Verifiable Quantum Advantage via Optimized DQI Circuits

Tanuj Khattar Corresponding author: tanujkhattar4@gmail.com Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Venice, CA 90291    Noah Shutty Corresponding author: shutty@google.com Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Venice, CA 90291    Craig Gidney Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Venice, CA 90291    Adam Zalcman Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Venice, CA 90291    Noureldin Yosri Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Venice, CA 90291    Dmitri Maslov Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Venice, CA 90291    Ryan Babbush Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Venice, CA 90291    Stephen P. Jordan Affiliation: Google Quantum AI, Venice, CA 90291
October 09, 2025
Abstract

Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) provides a framework for superpolynomial quantum speedups by reducing certain optimization problems to reversible decoding tasks. We apply DQI to the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem, whose dual code is Reed-Solomon (RS). We establish that DQI for OPI is the first known candidate for verifiable quantum advantage with optimal asymptotic speedup: solving instances with classical hardness O⁡(2N)O(2^{N}) requires only O~​(N)\widetilde{O}(N) quantum gates, matching the theoretical lower bound. Realizing this speedup requires highly efficient reversible RS decoders. We introduce novel quantum circuits for the Extended Euclidean Algorithm, the decoder’s bottleneck. Our techniques, including a new representation for implicit Bézout coefficient access, and optimized in-place architectures, reduce the leading-order space complexity to the theoretical minimum of 2​n​b2nb qubits while significantly lowering gate counts. These improvements are broadly applicable, including to Shor’s algorithm for the discrete logarithm. We analyze OPI over binary extension fields G​F​(2b)GF(2^{b}), assess hardness against new classical attacks, and identify resilient instances. Our resource estimates show that classically intractable OPI instances (requiring >1023>10^{23} classical trials) can be solved with approximately 5.72 million Toffoli gates. This is substantially less than the count required for breaking RSA-2048, positioning DQI as a compelling candidate for practical, verifiable quantum advantage.

Data availability: Code and assets created for this paper are available on Zenodo [1].

I Introduction

The pursuit of verifiable quantum advantage is a central goal in quantum computing. Quantum advantage refers to solving problems efficiently on a quantum computer where no efficient classical algorithm is known. Verifiability implies we can efficiently check the solution on a classical computer. Verifiable quantum advantage problems are a useful model of future applications of quantum computers to classical search and optimization problems abundant in industry.

A fundamental question in this pursuit concerns the efficiency of the quantum speedup itself. Given a problem instance with a target classical hardness of O⁡(2N)O(2^{N}) (where NN is the security parameter), what is the required quantum runtime? The theoretical lower bound is Ω⁡(N)\Omega(N) quantum gates [2]. However, existing candidates for verifiable superpolynomial advantage exceed this bound. For example, achieving O⁡(2N)O(2^{N}) hardness in integer factorization requires Shor’s algorithm [3] to use O~​(N6)\widetilde{O}(N^{6}) gates (against the General Number Field Sieve), while Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) requires O~​(N2)\widetilde{O}(N^{2}) gates (against Pollard Rho).

One corollary of the resource estimation performed in this work is to demonstrate that Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) [4], when applied to the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem, is the first known candidate for verifiable quantum advantage that achieves the optimal asymptotic speedup (up to polylogarithmic factors), requiring only O~​(N)\widetilde{O}(N) quantum gates to solve instances with O⁡(2N)O(2^{N}) classical hardness:

Theorem I.1.

There is an NP-search / optimization problem where the runtime of the best-known classical algorithm for the problem is 2N2^{N} and which can be solved with a circuit of O~​(N)\widetilde{O}(N) quantum gates.

We prove this theorem in Section IV. We compare this against prior speedups based on Shor’s algorithm in Table 1.

To understand how DQI achieves this speedup, we must formalize the class of problems it addresses. DQI provides a framework for approximating solutions to constraint satisfaction problems, specifically max-LINSAT, where its efficiency is tied to the efficiency of reversibly decoding a related error-correcting code.

Definition I.2 (max-LINSAT [4]).

Let 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} be a finite field. Given an m×nm\times n matrix BB over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} (with m>nm>n), and for each constraint i=1,2,…,mi=1,2,\dots,m, a subset Fi⊂𝔽qF_{i}\subset\mathbb{F}_{q}. The max-LINSAT problem is to find an assignment x∈𝔽qnx\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} that maximizes the number of satisfied constraints, where the ii-th constraint is satisfied if ∑j=1nBi​j​xj∈Fi\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}x_{j}\in F_{i}.

The DQI algorithm addresses max-LINSAT by defining a related objective function, f⁡(x)f(x), as the number of satisfied constraints minus the number of unsatisfied constraints. This can be expressed as:

f⁡(x)=∑i=1mfi​(∑j=1nBi​j​xj),wherefi​(y)={+1if ​y∈Fi−1if ​y∉Fi.f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}x_{j}\right),\quad\text{where}\quad f_{i}(y)=\begin{cases}+1&\text{if }y\in F_{i}\\ -1&\text{if }y\notin F_{i}\end{cases}. (1)

Maximizing f⁡(x)f(x) is equivalent to maximizing the number of satisfied constraints. The DQI algorithm works by preparing a quantum state |P⁡(f)⟩=∑xP⁡(f⁡(x))​|x⟩|P(f)\rangle=\sum_{x}P(f(x))|x\rangle, where PP is a polynomial of degree ℓ\ell designed to enhance the amplitudes of states |x⟩\ket{x} where f⁡(x)f(x) is large. The core insight of DQI is that the preparation of this state can be reduced to a decoding problem on the dual code C⟂={d∈𝔽qm:BT​d=0}C^{\perp}=\{d\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{m}:B^{T}d=0\}. The algorithm involves creating a superposition of errors ee and their syndromes BT​eB^{T}e. To achieve the necessary interference that amplifies good solutions, the error register |e⟩|e\rangle must be coherently uncomputed, which necessitates a reversible quantum implementation of a decoder for C⟂C^{\perp}. The performance of DQI is directly tied to the error-correction capability of this decoder. The degree ℓ\ell of the enhancing polynomial PP corresponds to the maximum number of errors the decoder must correct. A key result of the DQI framework [4] is the semicircle law, which provides a rigorous performance guarantee based on the decoding capability.

Theorem I.3 (DQI Semicircle Law (Informal) [4]).

Given a max-LINSAT instance where the allowed sets FiF_{i} have size rr over a field of size qq. If the dual code C⟂C^{\perp} can be efficiently decoded up to ℓ\ell errors, DQI can sample solutions that satisfy an expected fraction of constraints ⟨s⟩/m\langle s\rangle/m approaching:

(ℓm​(1−rq)+(1−ℓm)​rq)2.\left(\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{m}\left(1-\frac{r}{q}\right)}+\sqrt{\left(1-\frac{\ell}{m}\right)\frac{r}{q}}\right)^{2}. (2)

This theorem formalizes the intuition that a better decoder (a larger correctable error fraction ℓ/m\ell/m) leads to a better optimization result. Consequently, the efficiency of the reversible decoder dominates the resource requirements of the entire DQI algorithm.

In this work, we focus on constructing efficient quantum circuits for DQI applied to the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem, identified in [4] as a candidate for superpolynomial quantum speedup.

Definition I.4 (Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI)).

Let 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} be a finite field and n<q−1n<q-1. Given m=q−1m=q-1 subsets Fy⊂𝔽qF_{y}\subset\mathbb{F}_{q} for each y∈𝔽q∗y\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}, find a polynomial Q∈𝔽q​[y]Q\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[y] of degree at most n−1n-1 that maximizes the objective function: fOPI​(Q)=|{y∈𝔽q∗:Q⁡(y)∈Fy}|f_{\text{OPI}}(Q)=|\{y\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}:Q(y)\in F_{y}\}|.

When OPI is cast as max-LINSAT, the constraint matrix BB is a Vandermonde matrix, implying the dual code C⟂C^{\perp} is a Reed-Solomon (RS) code. For OPI, DQI can achieve approximation ratios that appear beyond the reach of known polynomial-time classical algorithms [4]. RS codes possess efficient classical decoders, such as the Berlekamp-Massey decoder [6] or the Extended Euclidean Algorithm (EEA) [7]. Our primary contribution is the development of highly optimized, reversible quantum circuits for syndrome decoding of Reed-Solomon codes using Extended Euclidean Algorithm-based decoders. We introduce several key strategies to minimize the quantum resources required:

  1. 1.

    Analysis of OPI over Binary Extension Fields: We shift the analysis from prime fields to binary extension fields, GF​(2b)\text{GF}(2^{b}). This choice significantly reduces the cost of the underlying quantum arithmetic (leveraging techniques like Karatsuba multiplication [8, 9] and Itoh-Tsujii inversion [10, 9]). Crucially, we analyze the classical hardness in this setting, confirming that the problem remains intractable against known classical attacks like Prange’s algorithm [11] and a novel variant, the Extended Prange’s algorithm (XP), tailored for extension fields.

  2. 2.

    Optimized Quantum Circuits for the Extended Euclidean Algorithm: We introduce two distinct compilation strategies for the EEA, each achieving minimal qubit overhead while being tailored for different algorithmic requirements. These strategies are general and shall offer substantial improvements for other quantum algorithms utilizing the EEA, such as those in elliptic curve cryptography [12, 13, 14] and DQI with EEA-based decoders for other codes like algebraic geometry codes [15] and RS codes with prime fields [4].

    • •

      For scenarios requiring explicit access to the Bézout coefficients, we present an improved synchronized circuit for the classic Euclidean algorithm [16, 12]. By storing quotients in-place within shared registers and merging arithmetic cycles, we deterministically achieve a leading-order space complexity of 2​n​b2nb qubits and substantially reduce gate counts.

    • •

      For scenarios where implicit access is sufficient, we introduce the novel Dialog representation. This data structure records the execution trace of a constant-time EEA, allowing our circuits to capitalize on the low gate costs of modern, division-free EEA algorithms [17] without incurring their typically large qubit overhead [14, 18].

  3. 3.

    Holistic Reversible Reed-Solomon Decoder Design: We construct end-to-end reversible quantum circuits for the full RS decoder that integrate our optimized EEA modules. Our design is compatible with both the explicit and implicit EEA approaches and fully accounts for the resource costs of the subsequent decoding stages—Chien Search and Forney’s algorithm—when operating on the compact, shared-register data structures produced by our EEA implementations.

We synthesize these techniques to construct end-to-end quantum circuits and provide detailed resource estimates using Qualtran [19]. Our results demonstrate that classically intractable instances of OPI (requiring >1023>10^{23} classical trials) can be solved with modest quantum resources. For instance, an (m=4095,n=70,b=12)(m=4095,n=70,b=12) instance requires approximately 5.72×1065.72\times 10^{6} Toffoli gates and 18851885 logical qubits. This is roughly 1000​𝐱1000\mathbf{x} fewer Toffolis than that required for factoring 2048-bit RSA integers [20], suggesting that DQI may offer a compelling near-term path to practical, verifiable quantum advantage in optimization. We also provide a physical resource estimate showing that the (m=4095,n=70,b=12)(m=4095,n=70,b=12) OPI instance can be solved using eight hundred thousand physical qubits and 11 hour of runtime under standard assumptions for superconducting architectures: a square grid of qubits with nearest neighbor connections, a uniform gate error rate of 0.1%, a surface code cycle time of 1 microsecond, and a control system reaction time of 10 microseconds.

II Methods for Optimized Implementation

We begin by presenting an improved, space-efficient construction of the DQI quantum circuit. We then present new techniques for compiling the Extended Euclidean Algorithm (EEA) for the two regimes—first, where one needs to explicitly compute the Bézout coefficients in memory, and second, where an implicit access to the Bézout coefficients is sufficient. For both scenarios, our goal is to find a construction that minimizes the qubit counts. For the first case, we make several improvements to the classical reversible EEA construction by [12, 16], resulting in lower qubit and gate counts. For the second case, we first formalize the idea of having implicit access to the Bézout coefficients and show how one can take advantage of the low gate counts for constant-time division-free variants of EEA [21, 17] while avoiding the high ancilla overhead. In both cases, we achieve the theoretical minimum leading order space complexity of 2​n​b+𝒪⁡(log2⁡(n))2nb+\mathcal{O}(\log_{2}(n)). We believe these improved techniques for compiling the Extended Euclidean Algorithm will be useful beyond DQI, especially in the context of Elliptic Curve Cryptography [14, 22]. We then specialize the discussion to the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem over binary extension fields, motivated by the fact that arithmetic circuits over binary extension fields are significantly cheaper to compile. In the end, we show how the decoding problem for Reed-Solomon codes can be solved using the Extended Euclidean Algorithm, along with other subroutines like Chien Search [23] and Forney’s algorithm [24]. We present optimized quantum circuits to account for the cost of these subroutines. Table 2 provides a reference for the key parameters used throughout our analysis.

II.1 The DQI Quantum Circuit: An Improved Construction for Qubit Efficiency

The goal of the Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) circuit is to efficiently prepare the state |P⁡(f)⟩=∑xP⁡(f⁡(x))​|x⟩|P(f)\rangle=\sum_{x}P(f(x))|x\rangle, where PP is an appropriately normalized degree-ℓ\ell polynomial. In the original construction[4, Section-8], the algorithm requires simultaneous instantiation of an m​bmb-sized error register, to hold a superposition of error patterns e∈𝔽qme\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{m}, and an n​bnb-sized syndrome register to hold the syndrome values s=BT​es=B^{T}e. This leads to a total space complexity of (m+n)​b(m+n)b plus the ancilla overhead due to reversible decoding. Note that the decoding problem is defined on an input of size n​bnb (the length of the syndrome), and hence for the regime where m≫nm\gg n, the multiplicative m​bmb qubit overhead in the DQI circuit is prohibitive.

We present an optimized circuit construction that significantly reduces qubit overhead by reformulating the Dicke state preparation, syndrome computation, and reversible decoding steps (stages 1, 2 and 3). The Dicke states in the DQI circuit are used to encode the locations of ℓ<n2\ell<\frac{n}{2} errors in the length mm codeword. Instead of using a dense representation consisting of mm qubits, we use a sparse representation consisting of ℓ⋅⌈log2⁡m⌉≤ℓ⋅b\ell\cdot\lceil\log_{2}{m}\rceil\leq\ell\cdot b qubits to encode this information. We show how to efficiently prepare Sparse Dicke States in Appendix B. Next, instead of generating the entire m​bmb-qubit error state |e⟩|e\rangle to encode the values of errors at each of the mm locations in the codeword, we employ a sequential approach utilizing Measurement-Based Uncomputation (MBU) [25, 26]. We iterate through the mm constraints, generate one error symbol eie_{i} (of size bb qubits) at a time, update the syndrome register with its contribution, and immediately uncompute eie_{i} via measurement in the X-basis. This leads to phase errors that we later fix as part of the reversible decoding step, where we sequentially generate each decoded error term eie_{i} and apply a phase fixup using the measurement result cic_{i}. This allows us to reuse a single bb-qubit ancilla register for all error terms during state preparation. Using Sparse Dicke state preparation and sequential computation of the error terms, the ancilla cost for preparing the n​bnb-qubit syndrome register reduces to n​bnb qubits. We will later show how to perform the reversible decoding on the n​bnb-qubit syndrome register using n​b+𝒪⁡(log2⁡(n))nb+\mathcal{O}(\log_{2}(n)) ancilla qubits, thus achieving a total space cost of 2​n​b+𝒪⁡(log2⁡(n))2nb+\mathcal{O}(\log_{2}(n)) qubits.

The following description of the DQI quantum circuit is for the general max-LINSAT case over a Galois field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. The construction proceeds through four main stages. The evolution of the quantum state across these stages is summarized below, utilizing an error locator register (ℓ⋅b\ell\cdot b qubits), an error value register (bb qubits), and a syndrome register (n⋅bn\cdot b qubits). We omit normalization factors for clarity.

    ∑k=0lwk(mk)−1/2(∑1≤j1<j2<⋯<jk≤mjk+1​…​jℓ=0|j1⟩b|j2⟩b⋯|jℓ⟩b)\sum_{k=0}^{l}w_{k}\binom{m}{k}^{-1/2}\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j_{1}<j_{2}<\dots<j_{k}\leq m\\ j_{k+1}\dots j_{\ell}=0\end{subarray}}\ket{j_{1}}_{b}\ket{j_{2}}_{b}\cdots\ket{j_{\ell}}_{b}\right) (3)

    In Appendix B, we describe a way to prepare Sparse Dicke States using 2⋅k⋅log2⁡m2\cdot k\cdot\log_{2}{m} qubits and 𝒪(m.k+k2b2)\mathcal{O}(m.k+k^{2}b^{2}) gates. The sparse construction is useful in reducing the qubit counts for instances where n≪mn\ll m.

  • •

    Stage 2: Sequential Syndrome Computation and MBU: This stage translates the error locator register into a superposition of syndromes, using our space-efficient sequential approach.

    Defining the Constraint Encoding Gates GiG_{i}: The operations in this stage depend on the specific constraints of the optimization problem. Recall the objective function f⁡(𝐱)=∑i=1mfi​(𝐛i⋅𝐱)f(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}(\mathbf{b}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}) with fi:𝔽q→{+1,−1}f_{i}:\mathbb{F}_{q}\to\{+1,-1\}. As detailed in [4, Section 8.2.1], we find it convenient to work in terms of gig_{i}, which we define as fif_{i} shifted and rescaled such that:

    gi​(x):=fi​(x)−f¯c,g_{i}(x):=\frac{f_{i}(x)-\bar{f}}{c}, (4)

    where f¯\bar{f} is the average value of fif_{i} over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} and cc is a normalization constant. This standardization ensures that the Fourier transform of gig_{i}, denoted g~i​(e)\tilde{g}_{i}(e), vanishes at e=0e=0 and is normalized (∑e|g~i​(e)|2=1\sum_{e}|\tilde{g}_{i}(e)|^{2}=1). We then define an isometry GiG_{i}, which acts on a singe qubit yiy_{i} storing whether an error occurs at index ii or not, and maps it to a superposition over bb-qubit error terms that encode these Fourier coefficients:

    Gi​|0⟩=|0⟩b,Gi​|1⟩=∑e∈𝔽q,e≠0g~i​(e)​|e⟩b.G_{i}|0\rangle=|0\rangle_{b},\quad G_{i}|1\rangle=\sum_{e\in\mathbb{F}_{q},e\neq 0}\tilde{g}_{i}(e)|e\rangle_{b}. (5)

    Sequential Syndrome Computation: We now iterate ii from 11 to mm, utilizing a single bb-qubit ancilla register:

    • (2a)

      Check if marked in Sparse Dicke State: Check whether index ii is contained in the Sparse Dicke state and record the outcome in a qubit yiy_{i}. Naively, this requires performing a bb-bit comparison with each of the ℓ\ell registers per iteration, requiring a total of m⋅ℓ⋅bm\cdot\ell\cdot b gates across mm iterations. However, since we are sequentially comparing each of the ℓ\ell registers in the Sparse Dicke State with consecutive classical constants i=1,2,…,mi=1,2,\dots,m, we can use a unary iteration [30, 31] circuit to merge adjacent comparisons and get a total cost of m⋅ℓm\cdot\ell gates across all mm iterations.

    • (2b)

      Error Generation: Apply GiG_{i} on the ii-th qubit of the mask register |yi⟩\ket{y_{i}} to temporarily generate the ii’th error term |ei⟩b\ket{e_{i}}_{b} using the bb-qubit ancilla register.

    • (2c)

      Syndrome Update: Compute the contribution of eie_{i} to the syndrome register |s⟩\ket{s} by coherently adding bi⋅eib_{i}\cdot e_{i} to |s⟩\ket{s} (where bib_{i} is the ii-th column of BTB^{T}).

    • (2d)

      Measurement-Based Uncomputation: Immediately uncompute the ancilla |ei⟩\ket{e_{i}} using MBU [25, 26]. The bb qubits are measured in the X basis, recording the classical outcome cic_{i}. This resets the ancilla for the next iteration but introduces a known phase kickback (−1)ci⋅ei(-1)^{c_{i}\cdot e_{i}}.

    At the end of the iteration, we simply do a measurement-based uncomputation of the Sparse Dicke state and perform phase fixups corresponding to the error locations during the reversible decoding step. By reusing a single ancilla register across all mm iterations, we avoid the m​bmb-qubit overhead of the original DQI construction. The final state of the system is

    ∑k=0lwk(mk)​∑|e|=k(∏i=1mg~i​(ei)​(−1)ci.ei)​|BT​e⟩n​b.\sum_{k=0}^{l}\frac{w_{k}}{\sqrt{\binom{m}{k}}}\sum_{|e|=k}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m}\tilde{g}_{i}(e_{i})(-1)^{c_{i}.e_{i}}\right)|B^{T}e\rangle_{nb}. (6)
  • •

    Stage 3: Phase Fixups via Reversible Decoding: In the original DQI construction [4], a reversible decoder was used to uncompute the explicit error register |e⟩|e\rangle. In our construction, the error register was already uncomputed via MBU in Stage 2. However, we must now correct the phase errors (−1)c⋅e(-1)^{c\cdot e} introduced by the measurements. Here, we perform reversible decoding using the syndrome register |s⟩=|BT​e⟩|s\rangle=|B^{T}e\rangle. We sequentially compute each decoded error term eie_{i} and use the measurement results cic_{i} to fix the phase error (−1)ci.ei(-1)^{c_{i}.e_{i}}. For the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem, this requires a reversible implementation of a decoder for Reed-Solomon codes, like the Berlekamp-Massey algorithm [6] or the Extended Euclidean Algorithm-based decoder [7, 32]. The final state of the system after this step is:

    ∑k=0lwk(mk)​∑|e|=k(∏i=1mg~i​(ei))​|BT​e⟩n​b≡|P⁡(f)~⟩n​b\sum_{k=0}^{l}\frac{w_{k}}{\sqrt{\binom{m}{k}}}\sum_{|e|=k}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m}\tilde{g}_{i}(e_{i})\right)|B^{T}e\rangle_{nb}\equiv|\widetilde{P(f)}\rangle_{nb} (7)
  • •

    Stage 4: Final Transformation and Measurement: After the successful phase fixups, the syndrome register is left in a state that is the Quantum Fourier Transform of the desired output state. To obtain the final state, an Inverse Quantum Fourier Transform (IQFT) is applied to the nn qudits of the syndrome register. This produces the final DQI state:

    |P⁡(f)⟩=∑xP⁡(f⁡(x))​|x⟩.|P(f)\rangle=\sum_{x}P(f(x))|x\rangle. (8)

II.2 Efficient Quantum Circuits for Extended Euclidean Algorithm

The Extended Euclidean Algorithm (EEA) is a cornerstone of computational number theory and a critical subroutine in algorithms for both classical and quantum computing [33]. While often introduced for integers, its principles generalize to other Euclidean domains like univariate polynomials with coefficients in a finite field, which is relevant to Reed-Solomon decoding. Given two polynomials, A⁡(z)A(z) and B⁡(z)B(z), Euclid’s algorithm iteratively generates a sequence of remainder polynomials ri​(z)r_{i}(z) using the recurrence ri−2​(z)=ri−1​(z)​qi​(z)+ri​(z)r_{i-2}(z)=r_{i-1}(z)q_{i}(z)+r_{i}(z), where r−1​(z)=A​(z)r_{-1}(z)=A(z), r0​(z)=B​(z)r_{0}(z)=B(z) and the quotient qi​(z)q_{i}(z) is chosen such that deg⁡(ri​(x))<deg⁡(ri−1​(x))\deg(r_{i}(x))<\deg(r_{i-1}(x)). The EEA is an extension to Euclid’s algorithm, which, alongside this sequence, also maintains two corresponding cofactor sequences, ui​(z)u_{i}(z) and vi​(z)v_{i}(z), that are updated at each step to preserve a crucial linear relationship known as Bézout’s identity. At every iteration ii, the triplet (ri​(z),ui​(z),vi​(z))(r_{i}(z),u_{i}(z),v_{i}(z)) satisfies the invariant:

A⁡(z)​ui​(z)+B⁡(z)​vi​(z)=ri​(z).A(z)u_{i}(z)+B(z)v_{i}(z)=r_{i}(z). (9)

This process is guaranteed to terminate because the degree of the remainder polynomial, deg⁡(ri​(z))\deg(r_{i}(z)), is a non-negative integer that strictly decreases with each iteration. The algorithm stops when the remainder rm​(z)r_{m}(z) becomes the zero polynomial. At this point, the previous remainder, rm−1​(z)r_{m-1}(z), is the gcd⁡(A⁡(z),B⁡(z))\gcd(A(z),B(z)), and the corresponding cofactors um−1​(z)u_{m-1}(z) and vm−1​(z)v_{m-1}(z) are the final Bézout coefficients.

Each step of the EEA can be expressed as an application of a 2×22\times 2 transition matrix τi\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{i} on the vector [ri−2,ri−1]T[r_{i-2},r_{i-1}]^{T}. The product of the first ii transition matrices store the Bézout coefficients uiu_{i}, ui−1u_{i-1} and viv_{i}, vi−1v_{i-1}. This matrix representation of the EEA will be useful as we describe our new constructions below.

(ri−1ri)=(011−qi)⏟τi​(ri−2ri−1)\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}r_{i-1}\\ r_{i}\end{pmatrix}=\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&-q_{i}\end{pmatrix}}_{\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{i}}\begin{pmatrix}r_{i-2}\\ r_{i-1}\end{pmatrix} (vi−1vi)=τi​(vi−2vi−1)\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}v_{i-1}\\ v_{i}\end{pmatrix}=\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{i}}\begin{pmatrix}v_{i-2}\\ v_{i-1}\end{pmatrix} (ui−1ui)=τi​(ui−2ui−1)\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}u_{i-1}\\ u_{i}\end{pmatrix}=\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{i}}\begin{pmatrix}u_{i-2}\\ u_{i-1}\end{pmatrix} (10)
τtotal=τm⋅τm−1​…​τ1=(um−1vm−1umvm)\displaystyle\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}=\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{m}\cdot\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{m-1}\dots\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}u_{m-1}&v_{m-1}\\ u_{m}&v_{m}\end{pmatrix} (gcd⁡(A,B)0)=τtotal​(AB)\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\gcd(A,B)\\ 0\end{pmatrix}=\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}\begin{pmatrix}A\\ B\end{pmatrix} (11)

One important application of the Extended Euclidean Algorithm is to compute multiplicative inverses in a finite field 𝔽q≅𝔽p​[z]/P⁡(z)\mathbb{F}_{q}\cong\mathbb{F}_{p}[z]/P(z), where P⁡(z)P(z) is an irreducible polynomial. To find the inverse of a polynomial A⁡(z)A(z), one applies the EEA to P⁡(z)P(z) and A⁡(z)A(z). This yields cofactor polynomials u⁡(z)u(z) and v⁡(z)v(z) such that P⁡(z)​u​(z)+A⁡(z)​v​(z)=gcd⁡(P⁡(z),A⁡(z))=1P(z)u(z)+A(z)v(z)=\gcd(P(z),A(z))=1. Taking this equation modulo P⁡(z)P(z) gives A⁡(z)​v​(z)≡1(modP⁡(z))A(z)v(z)\equiv 1\pmod{P(z)}, revealing that the Bézout coefficient v⁡(z)v(z) is the modular inverse. This operation is the principal computational bottleneck in Shor’s algorithm for Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), a cornerstone of modern public-key infrastructure. As a result, a significant body of research, summarized in Table 3 and Table 4, has been dedicated to designing resource-efficient quantum circuits for the EEA.

Early work by Proos and Zalka [16], Kaye and Zalka [12] showed that the standard Euclidean Algorithm based on polynomial long division is stepwise reversible and can be compiled using 3​n​b+𝒪⁡(log⁡n)3nb+\mathcal{O}(\log{n}) qubits using a register-sharing technique, where the registers holding the remainders and the Bézout coefficients are overlapped to use a total of 2​n​b2nb qubits and another n​bnb ancilla qubits are used to store the quotient in each iteration. By tolerating a small error, they show how to further reduce the qubit counts down to 2​n​b+𝒪⁡(log⁡n)2nb+\mathcal{O}(\log{n}), by using a 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log{n}) sized register to store the quotients since large quotients occur relatively rarely in the EEA. Their circuit design relies on a complex synchronization scheme, and they do not analyze the constant factors for gate counts. More recent works [13, 14, 18, 34] focus on using constant-time division-free variants of the Extended Euclidean Algorithm, like Binary GCD [21] and Bernstein-Yang GCD [17], to reduce the gate counts but suffer from significantly higher qubit counts because each iteration of these constant-time EEA algorithms is not stepwise reversible and generates additional garbage that leads to a higher ancilla overhead.

In this work, we provide two improved constructions for compiling the EEA, the first where the EEA explicitly computes the Bézout coefficients in memory, and the second where it suffices to have an implicit representation of Bézout coefficients. For both the constructions, we reduce the qubit counts to 2​n​b+𝒪⁡(log⁡n)2nb+\mathcal{O}(\log{n}), which is the best one can hope for given the input size is 2​n​b2nb, and our gate counts are lower than previous state of the art.

II.2.1 Explicit versus Implicit Access to Bézout Coefficients

A key theme of our work is the optimization of quantum circuits by carefully considering how the results of the EEA are used by the broader algorithm. We distinguish between two computational models: one requiring explicit access to the Bézout coefficients, and another where implicit access is sufficient. This distinction allows us to select the most resource-efficient EEA implementation for the task at hand.

As outlined at the beginning of this section, any execution of the EEA can be viewed as generating a sequence of 2×22\times 2 transition matrices, τ1,τ2,…,τm\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{1},\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{2},\dots,\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{m}. The product of these matrices, τtotal=τm⋅τm−1⋯τ1\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}=\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{m}\cdot\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{m-1}\cdots\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{1}, contains the final Bézout coefficients as its entries.

  • •

    Explicit Access: This is the conventional model, where the primary goal of the EEA circuit is to compute and store the full product matrix τtotal\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}. In the context of polynomial inputs, this means computing the coefficients of the final Bézout polynomials (e.g., vm−1​(z)v_{m-1}(z)) and storing them explicitly in a quantum register. This approach is necessary when the full polynomial is required for subsequent algebraic manipulations.

  • •

    Implicit Access. In this model, we avoid the costly step of multiplying the sequence of transition matrices. Instead, we only compute and store a compact representation of each individual matrix τi\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{i}. This metadata is sufficient to reconstruct and apply each τi\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{i} on the fly. The full Bézout coefficients are never materialized in memory but exist implicitly as the result of applying the sequence of stored transformations. Any operation requiring the Bézout coefficients is simply reformulated as a sequential application of the τi\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{i} matrices.

We illustrate the power of this implicit approach with two concrete examples:

  1. 1.

    Modular Polynomial Division: Consider the task of computing A⁡(z)​B​(z)−1(modP⁡(z))A(z)B(z)^{-1}\pmod{P(z)}, where P⁡(z)P(z) is an irreducible polynomial.

    • •

      The explicit “invert-then-multiply” approach first runs EEA​(P,B)\text{EEA}(P,B) to explicitly compute and store the inverse polynomial vm−1​(z)=B​(z)−1(modP⁡(z))v_{m-1}(z)=B(z)^{-1}\pmod{P(z)}. It then performs a separate quantum-quantum multiplication of A⁡(z)A(z) by this inverse polynomial.

    • •

      The implicit “direct division” approach instead runs EEA​(P,B)\text{EEA}(P,B) to generate the sequence of matrices τ1,τ2,…,τm\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{1},\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{2},\dots,\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{m}. To compute the division, it applies a sequence of matrix-vector multiplications to a different input vector, [0,A⁡(z)]T[0,A(z)]^{T}. The final state after applying τtotal\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}} is precisely [A⁡(z)​B​(z)−1,0]T(modP⁡(z))[A(z)B(z)^{-1},0]^{T}\pmod{P(z)}, avoiding the need to ever store the full inverse polynomial.

    We compare the costs of these approaches for modular division in Table 4.

  2. 2.

    Polynomial Evaluation: Consider evaluating the Bézout coefficient polynomial vm−1​(z)v_{m-1}(z) at a specific point γ∈𝔽q\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_{q}.

    • •

      With explicit access, one would use the stored coefficients of vm−1​(z)v_{m-1}(z) and perform a standard polynomial evaluation (e.g., via Horner’s method), requiring a series of quantum-classical multiplications.

    • •

      With implicit access, we first evaluate the simple polynomial entries within each transition matrix τi\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{i} at the point γ\gamma. This yields a sequence of constant 2×22\times 2 matrices with entries in 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. We then apply this sequence of constant matrices to an initial vector, such as [0,1]T[0,1]^{T}. The result of these operations over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} is the desired value, vm−1​(γ)v_{m-1}(\gamma). Once again, we did not ever store the full Bézout coefficient polynomial vm−1​(z)v_{m-1}(z) in memory.

Our work provides optimized circuits for both models. For explicit access, we improve upon the synchronized algorithm by Proos and Zalka [16], while for implicit access, we use the constant-time division-free variants of EEA [21, 17] as basis for the Dialog representation detailed in the following subsections.

II.2.2 Synchronized Reversible EEA for Explicit Bézout coefficients

We advance the synchronized register-sharing framework of Zalka et al. [16, 12] through two key innovations, resulting in an implementation that is both rigorously space-optimal and time-efficient.

First, we achieve the 2​N​b2Nb space bound deterministically via in-register quotient storage. Prior synchronized implementations utilized an auxiliary register for the quotient qq. To maintain low space overhead, this register was heuristically bounded to O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) qubits, incurring a fidelity loss for large quotients. We eliminate this auxiliary register entirely by utilizing the guaranteed available padding within the shared register (storing the pair (ui,ri)(u_{i},r_{i})) to temporarily store qi+1q_{i+1}. This makes the 2​N​b+O⁡(log⁡N)2Nb+O(\log N) space complexity rigorous, without relying on heuristics. Fig. 1 shows the evolution of the state of the system for each logical iteration of the synchronized Extended Euclidean Algorithm.

Second, we introduce a unified cycle architecture to reduce time complexity constants. The baseline synchronized approach cycles through four distinct circuit blocks (Division, Normalization, Bézout Update, Swap), leading to redundant arithmetic operations. For example, both the Division and Bézout Update step would need nn quantum-quantum multiplications and controlled additions each, even though for any step of the EEA these two cycles act on different parts of the shared registers storing the remainders and Bézout polynomials. In our unified architecture, a single, optimized circuit executes every cycle, with its behavior controlled by the synchronization counter. For example, our architecture integrates the arithmetic for Division and Bézout Update steps, such that a total of nn quantum-quantum multiplications and controlled additions are performed, effectively halving the dominant gate costs. Furthermore, we optimize the access to the in-register quotient by integrating localized CSWAPs within the sequential arithmetic loop, avoiding expensive generalized quantum addressing mechanisms.

In Appendix D we show that our synchronized reversible EEA requires 6​n6n iterations to terminate in the worst case. Fig. 9 in Appendix F gives a complete Python implementation that uses 2​n​b+𝒪⁡(log2⁡n)2nb+\mathcal{O}(\log_{2}{n}) space and nn quantum-quantum multiplications per iteration, resulting in the leading order gate cost of 6​n26n^{2} quantum-quantum multiplications.

II.2.3 Dialog Representation for Implicit Bézout coefficients

To understand the power of our implicit access model, it is useful to think not just about algorithms, but about different ways to represent mathematical objects. The familiar binary representation of an integer, for instance, is a list of 00 and 11 symbols. It is a representation (known since the square-and-multiply exponentiation algorithm) because the integer can be recreated from the symbols by initializing an accumulator to 00, and then iterating through the list of symbols and applying operations depending on the symbol (with ‘0’ meaning multiply accumulator by 2 and ‘1’ meaning multiply accumulator by 2 and add 1). The binary representation has many strengths. For example, digital logic circuits can implement the addition of binary integers in logarithmic depth. However, binary representation is not always the optimal choice. For example, carry-save adders use a slightly larger representation that enables performing addition in constant depth [35].

In this paper, we employ a different representation of numbers and polynomials. We call this representation the Dialog representation. Concretely, the Dialog is the sequence of transition matrices, τ1,τ2,…,τm\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{1},\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{2},\dots,\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{m}, generated by executing the Extended Euclidean Algorithm on the input pair A,BA,B. For constant-time division-free GCD algorithms [21, 17], this corresponds to a recording of the conditional branch decisions taken in each iteration. Abstractly, the Dialog is a decomposition of a pair of inputs (numbers or polynomials) into a series of small invertible matrix multiplications. This sequence is a valid representation because it provides a complete recipe to recover the original inputs from the output. Specifically, the total transformation τtotal=τm⋅τm−1⋯τ1\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}=\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{m}\cdot\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{m-1}\cdots\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{1} maps the input vector [A,B]T[A,B]^{T} to the output vector [gcd⁡(A,B),0]T[\gcd(A,B),0]^{T}. Consequently, applying the inverse transformation, τtotal−1\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}^{-1}, to the output recovers the original inputs.

(gcd⁡(A,B)0)=τtotal​(AB)=τm⋅τm−1​…​τ1⏟Dialog Representation​(AB)\begin{pmatrix}\gcd(A,B)\\ 0\end{pmatrix}=\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}\begin{pmatrix}A\\ B\end{pmatrix}=\underbrace{\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{m}\cdot\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{m-1}\dots\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{1}}_{\text{Dialog Representation}}\begin{pmatrix}A\\ B\end{pmatrix}
(umum−1)=τtotal​(10)\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}u_{m}\\ u_{m-1}\end{pmatrix}=\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix} (vmvm−1)=τtotal​(01)\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}v_{m}\\ v_{m-1}\end{pmatrix}=\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 1\end{pmatrix} (AB)=τtotal−1​(gcd⁡(A,B)0)\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}A\\ B\end{pmatrix}=\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}\gcd(A,B)\\ 0\end{pmatrix}
(um⋅Cum−1⋅C)=τtotal​(C0)\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}u_{m}\cdot C\\ u_{m-1}\cdot C\end{pmatrix}=\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}\begin{pmatrix}C\\ 0\end{pmatrix} (vm⋅Cvm−1⋅C)=τtotal​(0C)\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}v_{m}\cdot C\\ v_{m-1}\cdot C\end{pmatrix}=\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ C\end{pmatrix} (A⋅CB⋅C)=τtotal−1​(gcd⁡(A,B)⋅C0)\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}A\cdot C\\ B\cdot C\end{pmatrix}=\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}\gcd(A,B)\cdot C\\ 0\end{pmatrix}

Every symbol in the dialog representation must correspond to a small invertible matrix. When a representation has this property, we call it a linear representation. Note that the binary representation is not linear, because the ‘1’ symbol needs to increment the accumulator, and this action does not correspond to a matrix multiplication. The linearity of the dialog representation is a powerful property that allows us to perform complex algebraic manipulations by simply operating on the dialog itself. For example:

  • •

    Direct Modular Division and Multiplication: Since the transformation from inputs to outputs is linear, we can apply it to different vectors. To compute C⁡(z)​B​(z)−1(modP⁡(z))C(z)B(z)^{-1}\pmod{P(z)} where gcd⁡(P⁡(z),B⁡(z))=1\gcd(P(z),B(z))=1, we first compute the Dialog representation of (P⁡(z),B⁡(z))(P(z),B(z)). We can then apply the forward transformation τtotal\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}} to the scaled vector [0,C⁡(z)]T[0,C(z)]^{T}. By linearity, this directly yields the result [C⁡(z)​B​(z)−1,0]T(modP⁡(z))[C(z)B(z)^{-1},0]^{T}\pmod{P(z)} without ever materializing the inverse. Similarly, we can also perform modular multiplication by applying τtotal−1\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{\text{total}}^{-1} to the vector [C⁡(z),0]T[C(z),0]^{T} to obtain [0,B⁡(z)]T(modP⁡(z))[0,B(z)]^{T}\pmod{P(z)}.

  • •

    Evaluating the Bézout Polynomial: To evaluate the Bézout Polynomial vm​(z)v_{m}(z) at a point γ∈𝔽q\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_{q}, we can distribute the evaluation across the composition. We simply evaluate the polynomial entries of each transformation matrix τi​(z)\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{i}(z) at γ\gamma to get a sequence of constant matrices, and then multiply these constant matrices together.

This linear representation is most powerful when the transformation matrices τi\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{i} are themselves simple. For this reason, we construct the Dialog not from the classic EEA, but from constant-time, division-free algorithms like Bernstein-Yang [17], whose steps correspond to simple, constant-time matrix operations such as these:

  • •

    Doubling: The operation b⁡(z)←b⁡(z)/zb(z)\leftarrow b(z)/z corresponds to:

    Mdouble=(1001/z)M_{\text{double}}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1/z\end{pmatrix}
  • •

    Inversion: The operation (a⁡(z),b⁡(z))←(b⁡(z),a⁡(z))(a(z),b(z))\leftarrow(b(z),a(z)) corresponds to the matrix:

    Minvert=(0110)M_{\text{invert}}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}
  • •

    Addition: The operation b⁡(z)←b⁡(z)−c⋅a⁡(z)b(z)\leftarrow b(z)-c\cdot a(z), where c∈𝔽qc\in\mathbb{F}_{q}, corresponds to the matrix:

    Madd​(c)=(10−c1)M_{\text{add}}(c)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ -c&1\end{pmatrix}

In this case, the Dialog is simply the list of coefficients cic_{i} and the swap decisions from each step, such that it defines the ordered list of transformation matrices τi\scalebox{1.44}{$\tau$}_{i}. The name Dialog itself is a mnemonic for the core arithmetic operations involved: Doubling (or shifting), Inversion (or swap), and Addition/subtraction, and the representation is similar to a logarithm because it makes multiplication and division easy but addition and subtraction hard. For two input polynomials of degree up to n−1n-1, the Dialog consists of 2​n2n field elements.

A naïve quantum circuit for constructing the dialog would require 2​n​b2nb qubits to store and manipulate the remainder polynomials r−1=A(z),r0=B(z),r1,…rmr_{-1}=A(z),r_{0}=B(z),r_{1},\dots r_{m} and another 2​n​b2nb qubits to store the dialog, resulting in overall qubit count of 4​n​b+𝒪⁡(log2⁡n)4nb+\mathcal{O}(\log_{2}{n}). In order to reduce the qubit counts to 2​n​b+𝒪⁡(log2⁡n)2nb+\mathcal{O}(\log_{2}{n}), we once again use a register sharing technique by observing a key invariant of the constant-time EEA [17]: In each iteration, as one field element is computed and appended to the Dialog, the total number of coefficients required to represent the active polynomials, ri−1​(z)r_{i-1}(z) and ri​(z)r_{i}(z), decreases by one. This inverse relationship between the size of the Dialog and the size of the remaining polynomial data allows for an elegant quantum circuit that dynamically reclaims and repurposes qubits. Our construction uses a shared quantum register, poly, which stores the coefficients of the remainder polynomials ri−1​(z),ri​(z)r_{i-1}(z),r_{i}(z) and another quantum register, dialog, that stores the growing Dialog. At any point in time, we have the invariant: len(poly) + len(dialog) = 2n such that the total space occupied is 2​n​b+𝒪⁡(log2⁡n)2nb+\mathcal{O}(\log_{2}{n}). The architecture can be described as follows:

  1. 1.

    Initialization: The poly register is initialized to hold the coefficients of the two input polynomials, a⁡(z)a(z) and b⁡(z)b(z), stored from opposite ends of the register. This creates a layout with a central padded region:

    [a0,a1,…,ana,0,0,0,bnb,…,b1,b0][a_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{n_{a}},0,0,0,b_{n_{b}},\dots,b_{1},b_{0}]

  2. 2.

    Constant-Time Iteration Loop: The circuit proceeds for a fixed 2​n2n iterations, where nn is the maximum degree of the input polynomials. This ensures the algorithm completes for any input. Inside each iteration i=1,2,…,2​n1,2,\dots,2n:

    • •

      The control flow (e.g., the decision to swap the logical polynomials) is managed by the integer delta and the constant term of b⁡(z)b(z) (i.e., poly[-1]). A swap is performed by efficiently reversing the entire poly register, an operation implementable with a sequence of len(poly)// 2 CSWAP gates.

    • •

      The field element coeff for the update step is calculated from the constant terms of the active polynomials (poly[0] and poly[-1]).

    • •

      The polynomial subtraction, b⁡(z)←b⁡(z)−coeff⋅a⁡(z)b(z)\leftarrow b(z)-\text{coeff}\cdot a(z), is performed in-place. As per [17, Theorem A.1], after ii iterations, we have

      2​deg⁡(ak)≤2​d−1−i+δn\displaystyle 2\deg(a_{k})\leq 2d-1-i+\delta_{n}
      2​deg⁡(bk)≤2​d−1−i−δn\displaystyle 2\deg(b_{k})\leq 2d-1-i-\delta_{n}

      When coeff≠0\text{coeff}\neq 0, after the conditional swap, we always have δi≤0\delta_{i}\leq 0 such that deg⁡(b⁡(z))>deg⁡(a⁡(z))\deg(b(z))>\deg(a(z)). Thus, in the shared register representation, we perform poly[n - j - 1] -= coeff * poly[j] ∀j∈[0,len(poly)+δi2)\forall j\in[0,\frac{\text{len(poly)}+\delta_{i}}{2}).

    • •

      As a result of the subtraction and a subsequent logical right-shift of b⁡(z)b(z), the rightmost bb qubits of the register (previously holding b0b_{0}) become free.

    • •

      This newly freed block of bb qubits is immediately removed from the poly register and appended at the end of the dialog register, thus immediately re-purposing to store the computed coeff, which is the next element of the Dialog.

Crucially, at any intermediate step i of the algorithm, the poly and dialog registers contain a complete, holistic representation of the EEA’s state. The growing dialog register holds the partially constructed Dialog (from step 1 to i), while the shrinking poly register holds the coefficients of the current remainder polynomials, ri−1​(z)r_{i-1}(z) and ri​(z)r_{i}(z). From these two registers of total size 2​n​b2nb, one can always reconstruct the full mathematical state: the remainders are available directly, and the corresponding Bézout coefficients, ui​(z)u_{i}(z) and vi​(z)v_{i}(z), can be computed by playing back the partial Dialog. After the full 2​n2n iterations, the original polynomials have been completely reduced, and the Dialog has expanded to occupy the entire 2​n​b2nb qubits. The final state of the system is the complete Dialog, from which the gcd and the final Bézout coefficients can be derived implicitly. This in-place architecture, detailed in Fig. 11 of Appendix F, successfully constructs the full Dialog representation using a leading-order qubit cost of only 2​n​b2nb.

II.3 Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) over binary extension fields

While the original DQI paper focused on the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem over prime fields 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, we now study the problem defined over binary extension fields, GF​(2b)\text{GF}(2^{b}). The primary motivation for this is the prospect of substantially more efficient quantum circuits. Arithmetic in fields of characteristic 2 is often less resource-intensive to implement on a quantum computer. For instance, addition is a simple bitwise XOR, implementable with a linear number of CNOT gates. Quantum-Classical multiplication and Squaring are linear reversible circuits that can also be implemented using only the CNOT gates. Quantum-quantum multiplication based on Karatsuba algorithm [8] uses 𝒪⁡(blog2⁡3)\mathcal{O}(b^{\log_{2}{3}}) Toffoli gates, 𝒪⁡(b2)\mathcal{O}(b^{2}) CNOT gates, and no ancilla. Inversion can be reduced to only 𝒪⁡(log2⁡b)\mathcal{O}(\log_{2}{b}) quantum-quantum multiplications, resulting in low Toffoli counts [36, 10]. Appendix C details our optimized implementations of arithmetic circuits for G​F​(2b)GF(2^{b}). This reduction in the cost of the underlying field arithmetic translates directly to lower resource requirements for the overall DQI algorithm.

The OPI problem and the DQI algorithm generalize naturally to this setting, as discussed in [4, Section 14]. The problem can be stated analogously:

Definition II.1 (OPI over GF​(2b)\text{GF}(2^{b})).

Let q=2bq=2^{b}. Given integers n<q−1n<q-1, an instance of the Optimal Polynomial Intersection problem over GF​(2b)\text{GF}(2^{b}) is as follows. For each non-zero element y∈𝔽q∗y\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}, let FyF_{y} be a subset of the finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. The problem is to find a polynomial Q∈𝔽q​[y]Q\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[y] of degree at most n−1n-1 that maximizes the objective function:

fO​P​I​(Q)=|{y∈𝔽q∗:Q⁡(y)∈Fy}|f_{OPI}(Q)=|\{y\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}:Q(y)\in F_{y}\}|

For a general OPI instance, the subsets FyF_{y} can be arbitrary. As described in Section II.1, implementing the DQI algorithm requires constructing constraint-encoding gates GiG_{i} that prepare a superposition related to these sets. For an arbitrary set FyF_{y}, this step would require a generic quantum state preparation, costing roughly 𝒪⁡(q)\mathcal{O}(q) gates for each of the mm constraints.

To reduce the gate cost of the constraint encoding step while maintaining the classical hardness of the problem, we focus our resource analysis on a specific, structured variant of OPI where the sets FyF_{y} are chosen to allow for highly efficient implementations of the GiG_{i} gates. Specifically, we introduce and analyze the Twisted Bent Target OPI (Definition III.5). In this variant, the sets FyF_{y} are constructed from Maiorana-McFarland bent functions. This structure ensures that each gate GiG_{i} can be implemented with a gate cost that scales as 𝒪⁡(log⁡q)\mathcal{O}(\log q) rather than O⁡(q)O(q).

II.4 Decoding Reed Solomon Codes using the Extended Euclidean Algorithm

Having developed efficient quantum circuits for the EEA under both explicit and implicit access models, we now apply them to the central challenge of our work: constructing a complete, reversible decoder for Reed-Solomon (RS) codes. This decoder is the computational core of the DQI algorithm when applied to the OPI problem. Syndrome decoding of Reed-Solomon codes addresses the problem of recovering an error pattern e=[e0,e1,…,em−1]e=[e_{0},e_{1},\dots,e_{m-1}], where each ei∈𝔽qe_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q} and the number of non-zero errors |e||e| is at most ℓ\ell. The input to the decoder is a list of known syndromes, which are represented as the coefficients of a syndrome polynomial, S⁡(z)=s0+s1​z+⋯+sn−1​zn−1S(z)=s_{0}+s_{1}z+\dots+s_{n-1}z^{n-1}. The full decoding procedure involves three main stages: first, solving the key equation using the EEA; second, finding the error locations using a Chien search; and third, finding the error values using Forney’s algorithm.

Solving the Key Equation:

The core of the decoding process is to solve the fundamental key equation, a polynomial congruence that relates the known S⁡(z)S(z) to two unknown polynomials: the error-locator polynomial σ⁡(z)\sigma(z) and the error-evaluator polynomial Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z):

σ⁡(z)​S​(z)≡Ω⁡(z)(modz2​ℓ).\sigma(z)S(z)\equiv\Omega(z)\pmod{z^{2\ell}}. (12)

Here, ℓ=n2\ell=\frac{n}{2} is the maximum number of errors that the code can correct, σ⁡(z)\sigma(z) is called the error-locator polynomial because its roots identify the error positions, and Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z) is called the error-evaluator polynomial and is used to find the error magnitudes [24, 6]. A unique solution exists if deg⁡(σ⁡(z))=|e|≤ℓ\deg(\sigma(z))=|e|\leq\ell and deg⁡(Ω⁡(z))<ℓ\deg(\Omega(z))<\ell.

This polynomial congruence can be solved using several algorithms, most notably the Berlekamp-Massey algorithm [6] or the Extended Euclidean Algorithm (EEA) [7]. To solve it using EEA, we apply the EEA to the two specific polynomials A⁡(z)=z2​ℓA(z)=z^{2\ell} and B⁡(z)=S⁡(z)B(z)=S(z). As established in the previous section, the EEA produces a sequence of remainders ri​(z)r_{i}(z) and corresponding Bézout coefficients ui​(z)u_{i}(z) and vi​(z)v_{i}(z) such that:

A⁡(z)​ui​(z)+B⁡(z)​vi​(z)=ri​(z).A(z)u_{i}(z)+B(z)v_{i}(z)=r_{i}(z). (13)

Taking this identity modulo A⁡(z)=z2​ℓA(z)=z^{2\ell}, the first term vanishes, leaving:

S⁡(z)​vi​(z)≡ri​(z)(modz2​ℓ).S(z)v_{i}(z)\equiv r_{i}(z)\pmod{z^{2\ell}}. (14)

This directly matches the form of the key equation Eq. 12, with σ​(z)∝vi​(z)\sigma(z)\propto v_{i}(z) and Ω​(z)∝ri​(z)\Omega(z)\propto r_{i}(z). The algorithm is halted at the first iteration ii where deg⁡(ri​(z))<ℓ\deg(r_{i}(z))<\ell, which guarantees that the degree constraints for a valid solution are met.

Our quantum circuits for EEA perform this first step using either the synchronized algorithm of Section II.2.2 for explicit access to both σ⁡(z)\sigma(z) and Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z), or the Dialog-based method of Section II.2.3 for implicit access to σ⁡(z)\sigma(z) and explicit access to Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z). The efficiency of the subsequent decoding stages depends on which model is used.

Chien Search and Forneys algorithm:

Once the key equation has been solved via the EEA, yielding the error-locator polynomial σ⁡(z)\sigma(z) and the error-evaluator polynomial Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z), the decoder proceeds in two final stages. First, the Chien search [23] finds the error locations by identifying the roots of σ⁡(z)\sigma(z). This is achieved by evaluating σ⁡(z)\sigma(z) at every non-zero element of the field, γj∈𝔽q∗\gamma_{j}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}. An error is located at position jj if σ⁡(γj−1)=0\sigma(\gamma_{j}^{-1})=0. Second, For each error location jj found by the Chien search, Forney’s algorithm [24] computes the corresponding error value eje_{j} using the formula:

ej=−Ω⁡(γj−1)σ′​(γj−1),e_{j}=-\frac{\Omega(\gamma_{j}^{-1})}{\sigma^{\prime}(\gamma_{j}^{-1})}, (15)

where σ′​(z)\sigma^{\prime}(z) is the formal derivative of σ⁡(z)\sigma(z). This requires evaluating both Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z) and σ′​(z)\sigma^{\prime}(z) at the point γj−1\gamma_{j}^{-1}, followed by a modular division.

The implementation of these two steps differs significantly between the access models. In the explicit model, the EEA provides the coefficients of σ⁡(z)\sigma(z) and Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z) directly. The Chien search and Forney’s algorithm then proceed by evaluating these polynomials (and the easily computed derivative σ′​(z)\sigma^{\prime}(z)) at each point γj−1\gamma_{j}^{-1} using nn quantum-classical multiplications per evaluation. In contrast, the implicit model provides the Dialog of length n=2​ℓn=2\ell for σ⁡(z)\sigma(z), while still providing Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z) explicitly as the final remainder. Here, evaluating σ⁡(γj−1)\sigma(\gamma_{j}^{-1}) and σ′​(γj−1)\sigma^{\prime}(\gamma_{j}^{-1}) is achieved by playing back the Dialog on an augmented state vector. Since differentiation is a linear operator, we can track the derivative through the sequence of linear transformations by applying the chain and product rules. This requires 2​n2n quantum-quantum multiplications and n/2n/2 quantum-classical multiplications per evaluation.

The quantum resource costs for these stages depend heavily on whether the explicit or implicit access model was used for the initial EEA step. The trade-off is summarized in Table 5. The dominant costs arise from sequences of Galois field multiplications, which are categorized as either quantum-quantum (QQ), where both operands are in quantum registers, or quantum-classical (QC), where one operand is a known classical value.

As the table shows, the choice of model creates a clear trade-off. In the typical regime for OPI where n≪mn\ll m, the complexity of both models is dominated by the O⁡(m​n)O(mn) terms from the Chien search and Forney’s algorithm. For the implicit model, the dominant cost is 2​m​n2mn quantum-quantum multiplications needed to evaluate σ⁡(z)\sigma(z) and its derivative via Dialog playback. For the explicit model, the dominant cost is m​nmn quantum-classical multiplications to evaluate the three required polynomials.

For circuits over binary extension fields, a quantum-classical multiplication in GF​(2b)\text{GF}(2^{b}) can be implemented very efficiently using only Clifford gates (a sequence of CNOTs), whereas a quantum-quantum multiplication requires non-Clifford resources (Toffoli gates). Therefore, for the parameter regimes we study, the explicit access approach is substantially cheaper, as its dominant cost has a much lower Toffoli complexity. However, this trade-off should be carefully re-evaluated for other applications, such as those over prime fields, where quantum-classical multiplication is also expensive.

III Classical Attacks on OPI

Suppose we have a max-LINSAT problem over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} with allowed sets F1,…,FmF_{1},\ldots,F_{m} of size |Fi|=r|F_{i}|=r. Prange’s algorithm [11] can be applied to this problem as follows. First, we subsample any nn constraints to enforce via a linear system on the nn variables. This system can then be solved with Gaussian elimination. Since we have disregarded the remaining m−nm-n constraints, we expect that roughly r/q⋅(m−n)r/q\cdot(m-n) will be satisfied by chance since each constraint is satisfied by rr of the qq. Thus, we get, in expectation, a solution that satisfies n+r/q⋅(m−n)n+r/q\cdot(m-n) clauses. Prange’s algorithm can be repeated to achieve any desired fraction of satisfied constraints, albeit potentially with an exponential overhead in the number of repetitions. This is the most efficient classical attack on OPI that we are aware of. In Section III.1, we comment on how Prange’s algorithm could be optimized and show how to estimate the runtime required to match DQI’s performance on a large supercomputer. Then in Section III.2, we explain an improvement to Prange’s algorithm over extension fields and the impact on the runtime estimates in Section V.

III.1 Optimizing Prange’s Algorithm

We first comment on how Gaussian elimination in Prange’s algorithm [11] can be optimized to avoid an n3n^{3} cost per attempt. First, we can bring the generator matrix G∈𝔽qn×mG\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times m} into row echelon form such that the leftmost nn columns form the identity matrix. We let 𝐞(1),𝐞(2),…,𝐞(n)∈Span⁡(G)\mathbf{e}^{(1)},\mathbf{e}^{(2)},\ldots,\mathbf{e}^{(n)}\in\mathrm{Span}(G) denote the rows of this row echelon form. We can then represent any codeword 𝐜\mathbf{c} as

𝐜=∑i=1nci​𝐞(i).\mathbf{c}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}\mathbf{e}^{(i)}. (16)

To iterate over the codewords that satisfy the first nn clauses, we can view the problem as iterating over the strings where the ci∈Fic_{i}\in F_{i} above. Assume each |Fi||F_{i}| has size at least 2. Then we can iterate over strings that satisfy the first nn clauses using a Gray code that only updates two of the first nn coordinates per iteration. Over 𝔽2b\mathbb{F}_{2^{b}}, this could be implemented as two vectorized SIMD operations per update.

The semicircle law of [4] states that DQI will satisfy tt clauses in expectation, where

t/m=(ℓm​(1−rq)+(1−ℓm)​rq)2.t/m=\left(\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{m}\left(1-\frac{r}{q}\right)}+\sqrt{\left(1-\frac{\ell}{m}\right)\frac{r}{q}}\right)^{2}. (17)

Suppose we apply the classical attack to find a solution satisfying at least tt of the mm clauses, where t>nt>n. The number of satisfied clauses is distributed binomially, and the probability of sampling such a solution is:

p⁡(t):=∑s=tm(m−ns−n)​(rq)s−n​(1−rq)m−s.p(t):=\sum_{s=t}^{m}\binom{m-n}{s-n}\left(\frac{r}{q}\right)^{s-n}\left(1-\frac{r}{q}\right)^{m-s}. (18)

To match this with the classical attack will take, in expectation, 1/p⁡(t)1/p(t) trials. We estimate the classical resources required for one trial, using the Frontier supercomputer as an example [37]. Frontier contains 37,632 AMD Instinct MI250X accelerators (i.e., GPUs). Each MI250x has 220 compute units (CUs) and runs at 1.7 GHz. Each CU has 4 SIMD lanes. So, we can imagine that with an optimized implementation, Frontier could potentially run this many trials of the heuristic in one day:

24×3600×12×37,632×220×4×1.7×109≈2.43×102124\times 3600\times\frac{1}{2}\times 37,632\times 220\times 4\times 1.7\times 10^{9}\approx 2.43\times 10^{21} (19)

Note that no networking is required for our classical attacks (i.e., they are embarrassingly parallel), so we could easily distribute the workload over the Internet to many independent machines that run at different times, in odd hours, etc.

III.2 Extended Prange’s Algorithm over Extension Fields

The eXtended Prange’s algorithm (XP) is a folklore algorithm alluded to in [38], although we do not know of a reference that fully formalizes it as a cryptanalytic attack. For simplicity, suppose F1=F2=…=Fm=FF_{1}=F_{2}=\ldots=F_{m}=F. Suppose q=pbq=p^{b} for prime pp. Let

ϕ:\displaystyle\phi: 𝔽pb↔𝔽pb\displaystyle\mathbb{F}_{p^{b}}\leftrightarrow\mathbb{F}_{p}^{b}
ϕ⁡(𝐱)\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{x}) =(tr(ζx):ζ∈ℬ)\displaystyle=\left(\mathrm{tr}\left(\zeta x\right):\zeta\in\mathcal{B}\right) (20)

denote the natural bijection from elements in 𝔽pb\mathbb{F}_{p^{b}} to vectors in 𝔽pb\mathbb{F}_{p}^{b}, where ℬ\mathcal{B} is any basis for 𝔽pb\mathbb{F}_{p^{b}} over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} and tr⁡(α)=∑i=0b−1αqi\mathrm{tr}(\alpha)=\sum_{i=0}^{b-1}\alpha^{q^{i}} is the field trace (See Ch. 2 of [39]). Let Aff⊆2𝔽pb\mathrm{Aff}\subseteq 2^{\mathbb{F}_{p}^{b}} denote the set of nonempty affine subspaces of 𝔽pb\mathbb{F}_{p}^{b}. For each codimension s∈{0,1,…,b}s\in\{0,1,\ldots,b\}, let As∈AffA_{s}\in\mathrm{Aff} denote the (b−s)(b-s)-dimensional affine subspace which has the largest intersection |A∩ϕ⁡(F)||A\cap\phi(F)| with the set ϕ⁡(F)\phi(F), and let P⁡[s]P[s] denote its fractional overlap by P⁡[s]:=|A∩ϕ⁡(F)||A|P[s]:=\frac{|A\cap\phi(F)|}{|A|}. The general idea is that if we “pay” ss affine constraints over the base field on one of the coordinates i∈[m]i\in[m], then we get to flip a P⁡[s]P[s]-biased coin that determines whether the iith constraint is satisfied. We have a budget of n⋅bn\cdot b base field constraints to spend. We call any budget-respecting strategy which assigns a value of ss to each coordinate ii an “XP Allocation Strategy”. We consider two such strategies below.

III.2.1 Expectation-Optimal XP Allocation Strategies via Linear Programming

We can use a randomized procedure to decide ss for each clause. For each clause, this strategy samples ss independently according to the discrete probability distribution psp_{s}. This distribution is constrained such that, on average, we use b​n/mbn/m 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}-linear constraints, meaning we are exactly within-budget. It can be optimized to get the maximum expected number of satisfied constraints by solving the following linear program (LP):

maximize\displaystyle\mathrm{maximize}\, ∑s=0bps​P​[s]\displaystyle\sum_{s=0}^{b}p_{s}P[s]
subject​to\displaystyle\mathrm{subject\,to}\, ∑s=0bps=1\displaystyle\sum_{s=0}^{b}p_{s}=1
and\displaystyle\mathrm{and}\, ∑s=0bs​ps≤b​n/m\displaystyle\sum_{s=0}^{b}sp_{s}\leq\nicefrac{{bn}}{{m}}
where\displaystyle\mathrm{where}\,\,\, ps∈[0,1]​∀s∈{0,…,b}.\displaystyle p_{s}\in[0,1]\,\,\,\,\,\forall s\in\{0,\ldots,b\}. (21)

The optimal value of the above LP gives the optimal expected fraction of satisfied constraints achieved by the XP. We recover the truncation heuristic when we replace Aff\mathrm{Aff} with the set 𝒯:={{e}:e∈𝔽q}∪{𝔽q}\mathcal{T}:=\{\{e\}:e\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\}\cup\{\mathbb{F}_{q}\}. There are exponentially many affine subspaces in bb, the degree of the field extension (e.g. when p=2p=2, |Aff|∼7.37⋅2(b+1)2/4|\mathrm{Aff}|\sim 7.37\cdot 2^{(b+1)^{2}/4}). But for p=2p=2 and b≤10b\leq 10, we have |Aff|<109|\mathrm{Aff}|<10^{9} and we can explicitly enumerate these to compute the P⁡[s]P[s] table and solve eq (21). Moreover, it seems unlikely we would really need to enumerate all the affine subspaces, since most of them will have small overlap with the set FF. Perhaps, using better heuristics or Fourier-analytic techniques, we could directly compute the optimal allocation in time poly⁡(q)\mathrm{poly}(q). The XP can sometimes achieve a significantly higher expected value than Prange’s algorithm. For example, over 𝔽4\mathbb{F}_{4} with |F|=2|F|=2 and n/m=1/2\nicefrac{{n}}{{m}}=1/2, XP has an expected value of 11, whereas Prange’s algorithm would give an expected value of 3/4\nicefrac{{3}}{{4}}.

III.2.2 Probability-Optimal XP Allocation Strategies via a Knapsack Solver

If tt is larger than the optimal expected fraction of satisfied constraints from eq (21), we may need to run the XP many times to obtain one sample that satisfies ≥t\geq t clauses. Rather than maximizing the expectation value, we should instead maximize the probability of obtaining a sample that satisfies ≥t\geq t clauses. The optimal-probability allocation is the solution to the following problem:

maximize\displaystyle\mathrm{maximize}\,\,\, ℙ⁡(∑i=1mXi≥t)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_{i}\geq t\right)
subject​to\displaystyle\mathrm{subject\,to}\,\,\, Xi∼Ber⁡(P⁡[si])\displaystyle X_{i}\sim\mathrm{Ber}(P[s_{i}])
∑i=1msi≤B\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}s_{i}\leq B
0≤si≤b\displaystyle 0\leq s_{i}\leq b (22)

This problem is non-convex, and the solution may not be the same as the allocation strategy from eq (21). To obtain good approximate solutions to equation (22), we use a dynamic programming algorithm explained in Appendix A.

III.2.3 Search for good target sets for OPI over binary extension fields

The choice of good target sets seems to be a nontrivial problem. For a fixed set size |F||F|, we want to make the overlaps P⁡[s]P[s] as small as possible for each s∈{0,…,b}s\in\{0,\ldots,b\}. This way, the XP allocation strategies of eq (21) and eq (22) will have lower optimal values, giving a larger classical runtime. Identifying the optimal such set FF or even the best attainable list of overlaps P⁡[s]P[s] appears to be an open problem. Some recent insight on a good way to choose FF came from [40], who performed algebraic cryptanalysis of the binary OPI problem in the case that FF is chosen as the solution set of a multivariate polynomial equation (i.e., an algebraic variety). They concluded that for their application, cubic or higher-degree varieties were required. This is because quadratic varieties contain many dimension b/2b/2 affine subspaces. They operated in a high-rate regime (specifically, n/m>7/8n/m>7/8) so that they could obtain an exact solution with their quantum algorithm. The problem that then arises is that these affine subspaces are so large that the number of linear equations sufficient to enforce them as constraints is small enough that a rate 1/21/2 code would already be able to satisfy every clause using XP. However, in our scenario, we propose to use DQI, which is an approximate optimization algorithm. This allows us to keep the rate n/mn/m significantly lower than in [40] (in fact, the space cost scaling is dominated by nn, so the lower the rate of the code, the better). Although we do not obtain exact solutions, we obtain better approximate optima than can be obtained in polynomial time by any algorithm known to us, which is sufficient to obtain the large speedups here.

In fact, we find that a particular quadratic variety is an excellent choice to get a quantum advantage. Specifically, we chose bent functions from the Maiorana-McFarland family. In more detail, let n=2​kn=2k. Let

Sk={(x1,…,xn)∈𝔽2n:∑i=1kxi​xi+k=1mod2}.S_{k}=\left\{(x_{1},...,x_{n})\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}:\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{i}x_{i+k}=1\mod 2\right\}. (23)

As we show in Section III.2.4, for any affine subspace A⊂𝔽2nA\subset\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} of dimension d=dimAd=\dim A, we have

|A∩Sk|≤{2dd<k2d−1+2k−2k≤d<2​k−122​k−2d=2​k−122​k−1−2k−1d=2​k.|A\cap S_{k}|\leq\begin{cases}2^{d}&d<k\\ 2^{d-1}+2^{k-2}&k\leq d<2k-1\\ 2^{2k-2}&d=2k-1\\ 2^{2k-1}-2^{k-1}&d=2k.\end{cases} (24)

This can be fed as input to the knapsack solver described in Appendix A.

III.2.4 Upper bounds on affine intersections of Maiorana-McFarland target sets

We have found a technical proof of the upper bounds in (24), although we believe a simpler proof may be possible. All the key concepts involved are present in the proof for affine spaces with k≤dimA<2​k−1k\leq\dim A<2k-1. Therefore, we defer the proofs of upper bounds for d<kd<k, d=2​k−1d=2k-1, and d=2​kd=2k to Appendix E and focus here on k≤d<2​k−1k\leq d<2k-1.

Let kk be a positive integer. We use the standard dot product ⟨x,y⟩:=∑i=1kxi​yi∈𝔽2\langle x,y\rangle:=\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{i}y_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{2} where x,y∈𝔽2kx,y\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k} to define

Rk:={(x,y)∈𝔽2k×𝔽2k:⟨x,y⟩=0}\displaystyle R_{k}:=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k}\times\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k}:\langle x,y\rangle=0\right\} (25)
Sk:={(x,y)∈𝔽2k×𝔽2k:⟨x,y⟩=1}\displaystyle S_{k}:=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k}\times\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k}:\langle x,y\rangle=1\right\} (26)

so that Rk∪Sk=𝔽22​kR_{k}\cup S_{k}=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k} and Rk∩Sk=∅R_{k}\cap S_{k}=\emptyset. We will use ⊔\sqcup to make simultaneous assertions about the union and intersection of two sets. Namely, we define X⊔Y=Z⇔(X∪Y=Z)∧(X∩Y=∅)X\sqcup Y=Z\iff(X\cup Y=Z)\,\land\,(X\cap Y=\emptyset) for any three sets XX, YY, and ZZ. Thus, Rk⊔Sk=𝔽22​kR_{k}\sqcup S_{k}=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}. In arguments below, we will make frequent use of the implication X⊔Y=Z⟹|X|+|Y|=|Z|X\sqcup Y=Z\implies|X|+|Y|=|Z|.

We begin by deriving recursive structure formulas that express the sets A∩RkA\cap R_{k} and A∩SkA\cap S_{k} as the disjoint union ⊔\sqcup of the sets of the form B∩Rk−1B\cap R_{k-1} and B∩Sk−1B\cap S_{k-1} for some affine subspaces B⊂𝔽22​k−2B\subset\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2}. To that end, we use two linear projections π0:𝔽22​k→𝔽22​k−2\pi_{0}:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} and π1:𝔽22​k→𝔽22\pi_{1}:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2} defined by

π0​(x​a​y​b)=x​y,π1​(x​a​y​b)=a​b\displaystyle\pi_{0}(xayb)=xy,\quad\pi_{1}(xayb)=ab (27)

where x,y∈𝔽2k−1x,y\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k-1} and a,b∈𝔽2a,b\in\mathbb{F}_{2} and where juxtaposition denotes concatenation. For a w∈𝔽22​kw\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}, we will refer to π0​(w)\pi_{0}(w) as the root of ww and to π1​(w)\pi_{1}(w) as the suffix of ww. The map (π0,π1):𝔽22​k→𝔽22​k−2×𝔽22(\pi_{0},\pi_{1}):\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2}\times\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2} is invertible. Its inverse is ⊗:𝔽22​k−2×𝔽22→𝔽22​k\otimes:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2}\times\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k} defined as

x​y⊗a​b=x​a​y​b\displaystyle xy\otimes ab=xayb (28)

where x,y∈𝔽2k−1x,y\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k-1} and a,b∈𝔽2a,b\in\mathbb{F}_{2} as before. For X⊂𝔽22​k−2X\subset\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2}, Y⊂𝔽22Y\subset\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2}, and s∈𝔽22s\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2}, we will write X⊗s={x⊗s|x∈X}X\otimes s=\{x\otimes s\,|\,x\in X\} and X⊗Y={x⊗y|x∈X,y∈Y}X\otimes Y=\{x\otimes y\,|\,x\in X,y\in Y\}. Note that |X⊗Y|=|X|⋅|Y||X\otimes Y|=|X|\cdot|Y|.

The recursive structure of A∩RkA\cap R_{k} and A∩SkA\cap S_{k} arises from

⟨x,y⟩=⟨π0​(x),π0​(y)⟩+⟨π1​(x),π1​(y)⟩\displaystyle\langle x,y\rangle=\langle\pi_{0}(x),\pi_{0}(y)\rangle+\langle\pi_{1}(x),\pi_{1}(y)\rangle (29)

where we slightly abused notation by using ⟨.,.⟩\langle.,.\rangle to refer to the dot product in three different vector spaces, 𝔽22​k\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}, 𝔽22​k−2\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2}, and 𝔽22\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2}. We now state and prove the recursive structure formulas.

Lemma III.1 (Recursive Structure Formulas).

For integers d≥k>1d\geq k>1, let AA be a dd-dimensional affine subspace of 𝔽22​k\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}. Then

A∩Rk=⨆σ∈F{(Aσ′∩Sk−1)⊗σifσ=11(Aσ′∩Rk−1)⊗σifσ≠11\displaystyle A\cap R_{k}=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in F}\begin{cases}(A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\sigma&\text{if}\quad\sigma=11\\ (A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\sigma&\text{if}\quad\sigma\neq 11\end{cases} (30)
A∩Sk=⨆σ∈F{(Aσ′∩Rk−1)⊗σifσ=11(Aσ′∩Sk−1)⊗σifσ≠11\displaystyle A\cap S_{k}=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in F}\begin{cases}(A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\sigma&\text{if}\quad\sigma=11\\ (A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\sigma&\text{if}\quad\sigma\neq 11\end{cases} (31)

where F=π1​(A)F=\pi_{1}(A) is an affine subspace of 𝔽22\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2} and the sets Aσ′⊂π0​(A)A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\subset\pi_{0}(A) are affine subspaces of 𝔽22​k−2\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} that arise as translations of the same linear subspace W′⊂𝔽22​k−2W^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} with dimW′=dimA−dimF\dim W^{\prime}=\dim A-\dim F.

Proof.

We can write A=a+VA=a+V where a∈𝔽22​ka\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k} is a fixed bit string and VV is a dd-dimensional linear subspace of 𝔽22​k\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}. Let ℬ={b1,…,bd}\mathcal{B}=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{d}\} be an arbitrary basis of VV. Suppose b1,b2∈ℬb_{1},b_{2}\in\mathcal{B} are two distinct bit strings with suffix 0101. Then b1+b2b_{1}+b_{2} has suffix 0000, so {b1+b2}∪ℬ∖{b2}\{b_{1}+b_{2}\}\cup\mathcal{B}\setminus\{b_{2}\} is another basis of VV with the number of elements with suffix 0101 reduced by one. By iterating this procedure, we can reduce the number of elements with suffix 0101 to at most one.

Similarly, we can reduce the number of basis elements with suffixes 1010 and 1111 to at most one. Moreover, if ℬ\mathcal{B} contains three elements with distinct nonzero suffixes, then we can replace one of them with an element with suffix 0000 by adding the other two elements to it. Thus, VV has a basis ℬ\mathcal{B} that takes one of the following three forms

ℬ={ℬ00ℬ00⊔{b}ℬ00⊔{b,c}\displaystyle\mathcal{B}=\begin{cases}\mathcal{B}_{00}\\ \mathcal{B}_{00}\sqcup\{b\}\\ \mathcal{B}_{00}\sqcup\{b,c\}\end{cases} (32)

where ℬ00\mathcal{B}_{00} consists of bit strings with suffix 0000 and b,cb,c are two bit strings with distinct nonzero suffixes.

Define F:=π1​(A)F:=\pi_{1}(A) as the set of suffixes of the elements of A=a+VA=a+V. The projector π1\pi_{1} is a linear map, so FF is an affine subspace of 𝔽22\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2} and therefore it has either one, two or four elements. Indeed,

ℬ=ℬ00\displaystyle\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}_{00} ⇔F={σ}\displaystyle\iff F=\{\sigma\} (33)
ℬ=ℬ00⊔{b}\displaystyle\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}_{00}\sqcup\{b\} ⇔F={σ,τ}\displaystyle\iff F=\{\sigma,\tau\} (34)
ℬ=ℬ00⊔{b,c}\displaystyle\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}_{00}\sqcup\{b,c\} ⇔F={00,01,10,11}\displaystyle\iff F=\{00,01,10,11\} (35)

where σ=π1​(a)\sigma=\pi_{1}(a) and τ=π1​(a+b)\tau=\pi_{1}(a+b).

For every suffix σ∈F\sigma\in F, let Aσ:=A∩π1−1​({σ})A_{\sigma}:=A\cap\pi_{1}^{-1}(\{\sigma\}) be the set of elements in AA with suffix σ\sigma and Aσ′:=π0​(Aσ)A_{\sigma}^{\prime}:=\pi_{0}(A_{\sigma}) the set of roots of those elements of AA. A singleton set is an affine space, the intersection of affine subspaces is an affine subspace, and π0\pi_{0}, π1\pi_{1} are linear maps, so AσA_{\sigma} and Aσ′A_{\sigma}^{\prime} are affine subspaces of 𝔽22​k\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k} and 𝔽22​k−2\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2}, respectively. We can express AA in terms of Aσ′A_{\sigma}^{\prime} for σ∈F\sigma\in F as

A=⨆σ∈FAσ=⨆σ∈Fπ0​(Aσ)⊗σ=⨆σ∈FAσ′⊗σ.\displaystyle A=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in F}A_{\sigma}=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in F}\pi_{0}(A_{\sigma})\otimes\sigma=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in F}A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\otimes\sigma. (36)

Define W:=span⁡(ℬ00)W:=\mathrm{span}(\mathcal{B}_{00}), so that Aσ=uσ+WA_{\sigma}=u_{\sigma}+W where uσ∈𝔽22​ku_{\sigma}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k} is any bit string in AA with suffix π1​(uσ)=σ\pi_{1}(u_{\sigma})=\sigma. Then, Aσ′=π0​(uσ)+W′A_{\sigma}^{\prime}=\pi_{0}(u_{\sigma})+W^{\prime} where W′:=π0​(W)W^{\prime}:=\pi_{0}(W). But π0\pi_{0} is a bijection on WW, so dimAσ′=dimW′=dimW=|ℬ00|\dim A_{\sigma}^{\prime}=\dim W^{\prime}=\dim W=|\mathcal{B}_{00}|.

Finally, intersecting both sides of (36) with RkR_{k} (respectively, SkS_{k}), we obtain

A∩Rk=⨆σ∈F{(Aσ′∩Sk−1)⊗σifσ=11(Aσ′∩Rk−1)⊗σifσ≠11\displaystyle A\cap R_{k}=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in F}\begin{cases}(A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\sigma&\text{if}\quad\sigma=11\\ (A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\sigma&\text{if}\quad\sigma\neq 11\end{cases} (37)
A∩Sk=⨆σ∈F{(Aσ′∩Rk−1)⊗σifσ=11(Aσ′∩Sk−1)⊗σifσ≠11\displaystyle A\cap S_{k}=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in F}\begin{cases}(A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\sigma&\text{if}\quad\sigma=11\\ (A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\sigma&\text{if}\quad\sigma\neq 11\end{cases} (38)

where we switch between RkR_{k} and SkS_{k} when σ=11\sigma=11 as needed in light of (29). ∎

Remark III.1.

The recursive structure formulas take five forms depending on 0≤dimF≤20\leq\dim F\leq 2 and on whether 11∈F11\in F.

  1. 1.

    If F={σ}F=\{\sigma\} with σ≠11\sigma\neq 11, then

    A∩Rk\displaystyle A\cap R_{k} =(Aσ′∩Rk−1)⊗σ\displaystyle=(A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\sigma (39)
    A∩Sk\displaystyle A\cap S_{k} =(Aσ′∩Sk−1)⊗σ.\displaystyle=(A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\sigma. (40)
  2. 2.

    If F={11}F=\{11\}, then

    A∩Rk\displaystyle A\cap R_{k} =(A11′∩Sk−1)⊗11\displaystyle=(A_{11}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes 11 (41)
    A∩Sk\displaystyle A\cap S_{k} =(A11′∩Rk−1)⊗11.\displaystyle=(A_{11}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes 11. (42)
  3. 3.

    If F={σ,τ}F=\{\sigma,\tau\} with 11∉F11\notin F and σ≠τ\sigma\neq\tau, then

    A∩Rk\displaystyle A\cap R_{k} =((Aσ′∩Rk−1)⊗σ)⊔((Aτ′∩Rk−1)⊗τ)\displaystyle=\left((A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\sigma\right)\sqcup\left((A_{\tau}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\tau\right) (43)
    A∩Sk\displaystyle A\cap S_{k} =((Aσ′∩Sk−1)⊗σ)⊔((Aτ′∩Sk−1)⊗τ).\displaystyle=\left((A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\sigma\right)\sqcup\left((A_{\tau}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\tau\right). (44)
  4. 4.

    If F={σ,11}F=\{\sigma,11\} with σ≠11\sigma\neq 11, then

    A∩Rk\displaystyle A\cap R_{k} =((Aσ′∩Rk−1)⊗σ)⊔((A11′∩Sk−1)⊗11)\displaystyle=\left((A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\sigma\right)\sqcup\left((A_{11}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes 11\right) (45)
    A∩Sk\displaystyle A\cap S_{k} =((Aσ′∩Sk−1)⊗σ)⊔((A11′∩Rk−1)⊗11).\displaystyle=\left((A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\sigma\right)\sqcup\left((A_{11}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes 11\right). (46)
  5. 5.

    If F={00,01,10,11}F=\{00,01,10,11\}, then

    A∩Rk=((A11′∩Sk−1)⊗11)⊔⨆σ∈{00,01,10}(Aσ′∩Rk−1)⊗σ\displaystyle A\cap R_{k}=((A_{11}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes 11)\sqcup\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in\{00,01,10\}}(A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\sigma (47)
    A∩Sk=((A11′∩Rk−1)⊗11)⊔⨆σ∈{00,01,10}(Aσ′∩Sk−1)⊗σ.\displaystyle A\cap S_{k}=((A_{11}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes 11)\sqcup\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in\{00,01,10\}}(A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\sigma. (48)

Lemma III.1 enables inductive proof of the upper bound on |A∩Rk||A\cap R_{k}| and |A∩Sk||A\cap S_{k}| for affine spaces with dimension dimA=2​k−1\dim A=2k-1, which we defer to Lemma E.3. Below, we prove that |A∩Rk|≤2d−1+2k−1|A\cap R_{k}|\leq 2^{d-1}+2^{k-1} and |A∩Sk|≤2d−1+2k−2|A\cap S_{k}|\leq 2^{d-1}+2^{k-2} for affine AA with k≤dimA<2​k−1k\leq\dim A<2k-1 which requires more sophisticated tools in addition to Lemma III.1. The right-hand sides 2d−1+2k−12^{d-1}+2^{k-1} and 2d−1+2k−22^{d-1}+2^{k-2} indicate that the cardinality of A∩SkA\cap S_{k} (respectively, A∩RkA\cap R_{k}) can exceed 12​|A|\frac{1}{2}|A| by at most 2k−22^{k-2} (respectively, 2k−12^{k-1}). Thus, |A∩Rk||A\cap R_{k}| can exceed 12​|A|\frac{1}{2}|A| by twice as much as |A∩Sk||A\cap S_{k}|, so if a recursive structure formula for A∩SkA\cap S_{k} contains both an A∩Rk−1A\cap R_{k-1} term and an A∩Sk−1A\cap S_{k-1} term, then a naive inductive argument fails. We refer to such formulas as mixed recursive structure formulas. They have either two or four terms

A∩Sk=\displaystyle A\cap S_{k}= ((Aσ′∩Sk−1)⊗00)⊔((A11′∩Rk−1)⊗11)\displaystyle\left((A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes 00\right)\sqcup\left((A_{11}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes 11\right) (49)
