A∩Sk=\displaystyle A\cap S_{k}= ((A00′∩Sk−1)⊗00)⊔((A01′∩Sk−1)⊗01)⊔((A10′∩Sk−1)⊗10)⊔((A11′∩Rk−1)⊗11).\displaystyle\left((A_{00}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes 00\right)\sqcup\left((A_{01}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes 01\right)\sqcup\left((A_{10}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes 10\right)\sqcup\left((A_{11}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes 11\right). (50)

These recursive structure formulas do not cause issues in the proof of Lemma E.3 where we work around the challenge by exploiting the fact that when dimA=2​k−1\dim A=2k-1 not all affine subspaces on the right hand side are distinct. To face a more general situation below, we will exploit hidden affine structures in certain combinations of sets of the form A∩Sk−1A\cap S_{k-1} and A∩Rk−1A\cap R_{k-1} that arise from the cancellation of quadratic terms in the indicator functions of these sets as they are combined together.

Let WW be a linear subspace of 𝔽22​k\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}. If a function ff from WW to the underlying field of scalars 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} is linear, then we will refer to ff as a linear functional. Let a∈𝔽22​ka\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k} and let A:=a+WA:=a+W be an affine subspace of 𝔽22​k\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}. If a function gg from AA to the underlying field of scalars 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} can be written as g⁡(a+w)=c+f⁡(w)g(a+w)=c+f(w) for some c∈𝔽2c\in\mathbb{F}_{2} and some linear functional ff, then we will refer to gg as an affine functional. The significance of affine functionals to our arguments derives from the way they partition their domain. If gg is a non-constant affine functional, then ff is a non-constant linear functional and f−1​(1)f^{-1}(1) is a coset of ker⁡f=f−1​(0)\ker f=f^{-1}(0). Therefore, |f−1​(0)|=|f−1​(1)||f^{-1}(0)|=|f^{-1}(1)|. But then also |g−1​(0)|=|g−1​(1)||g^{-1}(0)|=|g^{-1}(1)|. Thus, if g:A→𝔽2g:A\to\mathbb{F}_{2} is an affine functional, then each g−1​(0)g^{-1}(0) and g−1​(1)g^{-1}(1) is either empty or affine. Moreover, if both g−1​(0)g^{-1}(0) and g−1​(1)g^{-1}(1) are non-empty, then dimg−1​(0)=dimg−1​(1)=dimA−1\dim g^{-1}(0)=\dim g^{-1}(1)=\dim A-1.

In order to express the value of the indicator function 𝟙Sk:𝔽22​k→𝔽2\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}\to\mathbb{F}_{2} of SkS_{k}

𝟙Sk​(x):=∑i=1kxi​xk+i=⟨πL​(x),πR​(x)⟩\displaystyle\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{i}x_{k+i}=\langle\pi_{L}(x),\pi_{R}(x)\rangle (51)

on bit strings in an affine space A:=a+WA:=a+W, we introduce the (skew-)symmetric bilinear form ω:𝔽22​k→𝔽2\omega:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}

ω⁡(x,y):=∑i=1k(xi​yk+i+xk+i​yi)=⟨πL​(x),πR​(y)⟩+⟨πL​(y),πR​(x)⟩\displaystyle\omega(x,y):=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\left(x_{i}y_{k+i}+x_{k+i}y_{i}\right)=\langle\pi_{L}(x),\pi_{R}(y)\rangle+\langle\pi_{L}(y),\pi_{R}(x)\rangle (52)

where πL,πR:𝔽22​k→𝔽2k\pi_{L},\pi_{R}:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k} are linear projectors defined via

πL​(a​b)=a,πR​(a​b)=b\displaystyle\pi_{L}(ab)=a,\quad\pi_{R}(ab)=b (53)

for any a,b∈𝔽2ka,b\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k}. Indeed, we can express 𝟙Sk​(a+x)\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+x) for any x∈Wx\in W in terms of ω\omega as

𝟙Sk​(a+x)\displaystyle\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+x) =⟨aL+xL,aR+xR⟩=𝟙Sk​(a)+ω⁡(a,x)+𝟙Sk​(x)\displaystyle=\langle a_{L}+x_{L},a_{R}+x_{R}\rangle=\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a)+\omega(a,x)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(x) (54)

where aL:=πL​(a)a_{L}:=\pi_{L}(a), aR:=πR​(a)a_{R}:=\pi_{R}(a), xL:=πL​(x)x_{L}:=\pi_{L}(x), and xR:=πR​(x)x_{R}:=\pi_{R}(x). This way of writing 𝟙Sk\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}} allows us to construct affine subspaces from sets of the form A∩RkA\cap R_{k} and A∩SkA\cap S_{k} by arranging for the cancellation of the quadratic terms 𝟙Sk​(x)\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(x).

We can use these objects and their properties to prove Lemma III.2 and E.4 that enable us to express the right hand side of (49) and (50) in terms of cardinalities of sets involving Sk−1S_{k-1}, but no Rk−1R_{k-1}.

Lemma III.2 (Proxy expression for mixed recursive structure formulas with two terms).

Let kk be a positive integer and a1,a2∈𝔽22​ka_{1},a_{2}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}. For any two affine spaces A1:=a1+WA_{1}:=a_{1}+W and A2:=a2+WA_{2}:=a_{2}+W arising as translations of the same linear subspace W⊂𝔽22​kW\subset\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}, there exist two sets B1B_{1} and B2B_{2} each of which is either empty or affine and such that

|A1∩Rk|+|A2∩Sk|=|B1|+2⋅|B2∩Sk|\displaystyle|A_{1}\cap R_{k}|+|A_{2}\cap S_{k}|=|B_{1}|+2\cdot|B_{2}\cap S_{k}| (55)

and |B1|+|B2|=|W||B_{1}|+|B_{2}|=|W|.

Proof.

We begin by partitioning WW into four disjoint sets

Wr​r\displaystyle W_{rr} :={x∈W|(a1+x∈Rk)∧(a2+x∈Rk)}\displaystyle:=\{x\in W\,|\,(a_{1}+x\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a_{2}+x\in R_{k})\} (56)
Wr​s\displaystyle W_{rs} :={x∈W|(a1+x∈Rk)∧(a2+x∈Sk)}\displaystyle:=\{x\in W\,|\,(a_{1}+x\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a_{2}+x\in S_{k})\} (57)
Ws​r\displaystyle W_{sr} :={x∈W|(a1+x∈Sk)∧(a2+x∈Rk)}\displaystyle:=\{x\in W\,|\,(a_{1}+x\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a_{2}+x\in R_{k})\} (58)
Ws​s\displaystyle W_{ss} :={x∈W|(a1+x∈Sk)∧(a2+x∈Sk)}\displaystyle:=\{x\in W\,|\,(a_{1}+x\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a_{2}+x\in S_{k})\} (59)

so that W=Wr​r⊔Wr​s⊔Ws​r⊔Ws​sW=W_{rr}\sqcup W_{rs}\sqcup W_{sr}\sqcup W_{ss}. Consider the sets

W0:=Wr​r⊔Ws​sW1:=Wr​s⊔Ws​r.\displaystyle W_{0}:=W_{rr}\sqcup W_{ss}\quad W_{1}:=W_{rs}\sqcup W_{sr}. (60)

The indicator function of W1W_{1} restricted to WW can be written as

𝟙W1​(x)\displaystyle\mathbb{1}_{W_{1}}(x) =𝟙Rk​(a1+x)⋅𝟙Sk​(a2+x)+𝟙Sk​(a1+x)⋅𝟙Rk​(a2+x)\displaystyle=\mathbb{1}_{R_{k}}(a_{1}+x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a_{2}+x)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a_{1}+x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{R_{k}}(a_{2}+x) (61)
=(1+𝟙Sk​(a1+x))⋅𝟙Sk​(a2+x)+𝟙Sk​(a1+x)⋅(1+𝟙Sk​(a2+x))\displaystyle=\left(1+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a_{1}+x)\right)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a_{2}+x)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a_{1}+x)\cdot\left(1+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a_{2}+x)\right) (62)
=𝟙Sk​(a1+x)+𝟙Sk​(a2+x)\displaystyle=\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a_{1}+x)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a_{2}+x) (63)
=ω⁡(a1+a2,x)+𝟙Sk​(a1)+𝟙Sk​(a2)\displaystyle=\omega(a_{1}+a_{2},x)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a_{1})+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a_{2}) (64)

where we dropped the terms 𝟙Sk​(a1+x)⋅𝟙Sk​(a2+x)\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a_{1}+x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a_{2}+x) and 𝟙Sk​(x)\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(x), because 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} has characteristic 22. But ω\omega is bilinear, so 𝟙W1\mathbb{1}_{W_{1}} restricted to WW is an affine functional on WW. Therefore, W1W_{1} is either empty or an affine subspace of WW. Similarly, the indicator function of W0W_{0} restricted to WW is 𝟙W0​(x)=𝟙W1​(x)+1\mathbb{1}_{W_{0}}(x)=\mathbb{1}_{W_{1}}(x)+1 and hence also an affine functional on WW. Therefore, W0W_{0} is either empty or an affine subspace of WW. Moreover, W=W0⊔W1W=W_{0}\sqcup W_{1}, so if both W0W_{0} and W1W_{1} are non-empty, then dimW0=dimW1=dimW−1\dim W_{0}=\dim W_{1}=\dim W-1. Translation is bijective, so definitions (56)-(59) imply that

|A1∩Rk|+|A2∩Sk|=|Wr​r|+2⋅|Wr​s|+|Ws​s|.\displaystyle|A_{1}\cap R_{k}|+|A_{2}\cap S_{k}|=|W_{rr}|+2\cdot|W_{rs}|+|W_{ss}|. (65)

Finally, define B1:=a1+W0B_{1}:=a_{1}+W_{0} and B2:=a2+W1B_{2}:=a_{2}+W_{1}, so that |B1|+|B2|=|W0|+|W1|=|W||B_{1}|+|B_{2}|=|W_{0}|+|W_{1}|=|W| and rewrite (65) as

|A1∩Rk|+|A2∩Sk|=|B1|+2⋅|B2∩Sk|\displaystyle|A_{1}\cap R_{k}|+|A_{2}\cap S_{k}|=|B_{1}|+2\cdot|B_{2}\cap S_{k}| (66)

where we used |B1|=|Wr​r|+|Ws​s||B_{1}|=|W_{rr}|+|W_{ss}| and |Wr​s|=|B2∩Sk||W_{rs}|=|B_{2}\cap S_{k}|. ∎

In order to facilitate the use of Lemma III.2 in an inductive proof, we note the following conditional upper bound it implies.

Corollary III.1 (Bound for mixed recursive structure formulas with two terms).

Let ee and k>1k>1 be positive integers. If |B∩Sk−1|≤2dimB−1+2k−3|B\cap S_{k-1}|\leq 2^{\dim B-1}+2^{k-3} for every affine subspace BB of 𝔽22​k−2\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} with dimB∈{e−1,e}\dim B\in\{e-1,e\}, then

|A1∩Rk−1|+|A2∩Sk−1|≤2e+2k−2\displaystyle|A_{1}\cap R_{k-1}|+|A_{2}\cap S_{k-1}|\leq 2^{e}+2^{k-2} (67)

for every pair of ee-dimensional affine subspaces A1:=a1+WA_{1}:=a_{1}+W and A2:=a2+WA_{2}:=a_{2}+W of 𝔽22​k−2\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} that arise as translations of the same linear subspace WW of 𝔽22​k−2\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2}.

Proof.

By Lemma III.2, there exist two sets B1B_{1} and B2B_{2}, each of which is either empty or affine and such that

|A1∩Rk−1|+|A2∩Sk−1|=|B1|+2⋅|B2∩Sk−1|\displaystyle|A_{1}\cap R_{k-1}|+|A_{2}\cap S_{k-1}|=|B_{1}|+2\cdot|B_{2}\cap S_{k-1}| (68)

and |B1|+|B2|=|W||B_{1}|+|B_{2}|=|W|. If B1=∅B_{1}=\emptyset, then B2B_{2} is an affine subspace of 𝔽22​k−2\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} of dimension ee. Therefore,

|A1∩Rk−1|+|A2∩Sk−1|≤0+2⋅(2e−1+2k−3)=2e+2k−2.\displaystyle|A_{1}\cap R_{k-1}|+|A_{2}\cap S_{k-1}|\leq 0+2\cdot(2^{e-1}+2^{k-3})=2^{e}+2^{k-2}. (69)

If B2=∅B_{2}=\emptyset, then B1B_{1} is an affine subspace of 𝔽22​k−2\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} of dimension ee. Therefore,

|A1∩Rk−1|+|A2∩Sk−1|≤2e+2⋅0<2e+2k−2.\displaystyle|A_{1}\cap R_{k-1}|+|A_{2}\cap S_{k-1}|\leq 2^{e}+2\cdot 0<2^{e}+2^{k-2}. (70)

Finally, if neither B1B_{1} nor B2B_{2} is empty, then both are affine and dimB1=dimB2=e−1\dim B_{1}=\dim B_{2}=e-1. Therefore,

|A1∩Rk−1|+|A2∩Sk−1|≤2e−1+2⋅(2e−2+2k−3)=2e+2k−2\displaystyle|A_{1}\cap R_{k-1}|+|A_{2}\cap S_{k-1}|\leq 2^{e-1}+2\cdot(2^{e-2}+2^{k-3})=2^{e}+2^{k-2} (71)

completing the proof of the Corollary. ∎

A similar, although technically more complicated, proof establishes an analogous result for mixed recursive formulas with four terms, see Lemma E.4 and Corollary E.2. Equipped with Corollary III.1 above for dealing with two-term mixed recursive structure formulas and Corollary E.2 for dealing with four-term mixed recursive structure formulas, we are now ready to prove the upper bounds on |A∩Rk||A\cap R_{k}| and |A∩Sk||A\cap S_{k}| for affine spaces with k≤dimA<2​k−1k\leq\dim A<2k-1.

Lemma III.3 (Upper bound on |A∩Rk||A\cap R_{k}| and |A∩Sk||A\cap S_{k}| when k≤dimA<2​k−1k\leq\dim A<2k-1).

Let k,dk,d be two positive integers and let A⊂𝔽22​kA\subset\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k} be a dd-dimensional affine subspace of 𝔽22​k\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}. If k≤d<2​k−1k\leq d<2k-1, then

|A∩Rk|\displaystyle|A\cap R_{k}| ≤2d−1+2k−1\displaystyle\leq 2^{d-1}+2^{k-1} (72)
|A∩Sk|\displaystyle|A\cap S_{k}| ≤2d−1+2k−2.\displaystyle\leq 2^{d-1}+2^{k-2}. (73)
Proof.

We prove the bounds by induction on kk. If k=1k=1, then there are no affine subspaces of dimension 1≤dimA<11\leq\dim A<1, so the upper bounds are vacuously satisfied. Fix k>1k>1 and suppose that for any affine subspace B⊂𝔽22​k−2B\subset\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} whose dimension e:=dimBe:=\dim B satisfies k−1≤e<2​k−3k-1\leq e<2k-3, it is the case that

|B∩Rk−1|\displaystyle|B\cap R_{k-1}| ≤2e−1+2k−2\displaystyle\leq 2^{e-1}+2^{k-2} (74)
|B∩Sk−1|\displaystyle|B\cap S_{k-1}| ≤2e−1+2k−3.\displaystyle\leq 2^{e-1}+2^{k-3}. (75)

We will also use (74) and (75) when e=2​k−3e=2k-3 and e=2​k−2e=2k-2 which follow from Lemma E.3 and Corollary E.1, respectively. We will show that for every affine subspace A⊂𝔽22​kA\subset\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k} of dimension d=dimAd=\dim A with k≤d<2​k−1k\leq d<2k-1, we have

|A∩Rk|\displaystyle|A\cap R_{k}| ≤2d−1+2k−1\displaystyle\leq 2^{d-1}+2^{k-1} (76)
|A∩Sk|\displaystyle|A\cap S_{k}| ≤2d−1+2k−2.\displaystyle\leq 2^{d-1}+2^{k-2}. (77)

By Remark III.1, we have five cases to consider

dimF=0\displaystyle\dim F=0 ∧11∉F\displaystyle\quad\land\quad 11\notin F (78)
dimF=0\displaystyle\dim F=0 ∧11∈F\displaystyle\quad\land\quad 11\in F (79)
dimF=1\displaystyle\dim F=1 ∧11∉F\displaystyle\quad\land\quad 11\notin F (80)
dimF=1\displaystyle\dim F=1 ∧11∈F\displaystyle\quad\land\quad 11\in F (81)
dimF=2\displaystyle\dim F=2 . (82)

In the first case, where F={σ}F=\{\sigma\} with σ≠11\sigma\neq 11, the recursive structure formulas (30) and (31) become

A∩Rk\displaystyle A\cap R_{k} =(Aσ′∩Rk−1)⊗σ\displaystyle=(A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\sigma (83)
A∩Sk\displaystyle A\cap S_{k} =(Aσ′∩Sk−1)⊗σ\displaystyle=(A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\sigma (84)

where the affine subspace Aσ′A_{\sigma}^{\prime} has dimension dimAσ′=d−dimF=d\dim A_{\sigma}^{\prime}=d-\dim F=d. Using the inductive hypothesis, we obtain

|A∩Rk|\displaystyle|A\cap R_{k}| =|Aσ′∩Rk−1|≤2d−1+2k−2<2d−1+2k−1\displaystyle=|A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1}|\leq 2^{d-1}+2^{k-2}<2^{d-1}+2^{k-1} (85)
|A∩Sk|\displaystyle|A\cap S_{k}| =|Aσ′∩Sk−1|≤2d−1+2k−3<2d−1+2k−2.\displaystyle=|A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1}|\leq 2^{d-1}+2^{k-3}<2^{d-1}+2^{k-2}. (86)

In the second case, where F={11}F=\{11\}, the recursive structure formulas (30) and (31) become

A∩Rk\displaystyle A\cap R_{k} =(A11′∩Sk−1)⊗σ\displaystyle=(A_{11}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\sigma (87)
A∩Sk\displaystyle A\cap S_{k} =(A11′∩Rk−1)⊗σ\displaystyle=(A_{11}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\sigma (88)

where the affine subspace A11′A_{11}^{\prime} again has dimension dimA11′=d−dimF=d\dim A_{11}^{\prime}=d-\dim F=d. Using the inductive hypothesis, we find

|A∩Rk|\displaystyle|A\cap R_{k}| =|A11′∩Sk−1|≤2d−1+2k−3<2d−1+2k−1\displaystyle=|A_{11}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1}|\leq 2^{d-1}+2^{k-3}<2^{d-1}+2^{k-1} (89)
|A∩Sk|\displaystyle|A\cap S_{k}| =|A11′∩Rk−1|≤2d−1+2k−2=2d−1+2k−2.\displaystyle=|A_{11}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1}|\leq 2^{d-1}+2^{k-2}=2^{d-1}+2^{k-2}. (90)

In the third case, where F={σ,τ}F=\{\sigma,\tau\} with σ≠11\sigma\neq 11, τ≠11\tau\neq 11 and σ≠τ\sigma\neq\tau, the recursive structure formulas read

A∩Rk\displaystyle A\cap R_{k} =((Aσ′∩Rk−1)⊗σ)⊔((Aτ′∩Rk−1)⊗τ)\displaystyle=((A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\sigma)\sqcup((A_{\tau}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\tau) (91)
A∩Sk\displaystyle A\cap S_{k} =((Aσ′∩Sk−1)⊗σ)⊔((Aτ′∩Sk−1)⊗τ).\displaystyle=((A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\sigma)\sqcup((A_{\tau}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\tau). (92)

Using the inductive hypothesis and dimAσ′=dimAτ′=d−dimF=d−1\dim A_{\sigma}^{\prime}=\dim A_{\tau}^{\prime}=d-\dim F=d-1, we find

|A∩Rk|\displaystyle|A\cap R_{k}| ≤2⋅(2d−2+2k−2)=2d−1+2k−1\displaystyle\leq 2\cdot(2^{d-2}+2^{k-2})=2^{d-1}+2^{k-1} (93)
|A∩Sk|\displaystyle|A\cap S_{k}| ≤2⋅(2d−2+2k−3)=2d−1+2k−2.\displaystyle\leq 2\cdot(2^{d-2}+2^{k-3})=2^{d-1}+2^{k-2}. (94)

In the fourth case, where F={σ,11}F=\{\sigma,11\} with σ≠11\sigma\neq 11, the recursive structure formulas (30) and (31) become

A∩Rk\displaystyle A\cap R_{k} =((A11′∩Sk−1)⊗11)⊔((Aσ′∩Rk−1)⊗σ)\displaystyle=((A_{11}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes 11)\sqcup((A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes\sigma) (95)
A∩Sk\displaystyle A\cap S_{k} =((A11′∩Rk−1)⊗11)⊔((Aσ′∩Sk−1)⊗σ)\displaystyle=((A_{11}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes 11)\sqcup((A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes\sigma) (96)

where dimAσ′=dimA11′=d−dimF=d−1\dim A_{\sigma}^{\prime}=\dim A_{11}^{\prime}=d-\dim F=d-1. Consequently,

|A∩Rk|\displaystyle|A\cap R_{k}| =|A11′∩Sk−1|+|Aσ′∩Rk−1|\displaystyle=|A_{11}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1}| (97)
|A∩Sk|\displaystyle|A\cap S_{k}| =|A11′∩Rk−1|+|Aσ′∩Sk−1|.\displaystyle=|A_{11}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1}|+|A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1}|. (98)

We obtain the upper bound on |A∩Rk||A\cap R_{k}| from the inductive hypothesis

|A∩Rk|\displaystyle|A\cap R_{k}| ≤2d−2+2k−3+2d−2+2k−2<2d−1+2k−1\displaystyle\leq 2^{d-2}+2^{k-3}+2^{d-2}+2^{k-2}<2^{d-1}+2^{k-1} (99)

and the upper bound on |A∩Sk||A\cap S_{k}| using Corollary III.1 with e=d−1e=d-1

|A∩Sk|\displaystyle|A\cap S_{k}| =|A11′∩Rk−1|+|Aσ′∩Sk−1|≤2d−1+2k−2\displaystyle=|A_{11}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1}|+|A_{\sigma}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1}|\leq 2^{d-1}+2^{k-2} (100)

where the Corollary’s assumption follows from the inductive hypothesis and Lemma E.1.

Finally, in the fifth case, where F={00,01,10,11}F=\{00,01,10,11\}, the recursive structure formulas (30) and (31) become

A∩Rk=\displaystyle A\cap R_{k}= ((A00′∩Rk−1)⊗00)⊔((A01′∩Rk−1)⊗01)⊔((A10′∩Rk−1)⊗10)⊔((A11′∩Sk−1)⊗11)\displaystyle\left((A_{00}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes 00\right)\sqcup\left((A_{01}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes 01\right)\sqcup\left((A_{10}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes 10\right)\sqcup\left((A_{11}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes 11\right) (101)
A∩Sk=\displaystyle A\cap S_{k}= ((A00′∩Sk−1)⊗00)⊔((A01′∩Sk−1)⊗01)⊔((A10′∩Sk−1)⊗10)⊔((A11′∩Rk−1)⊗11).\displaystyle\left((A_{00}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes 00\right)\sqcup\left((A_{01}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes 01\right)\sqcup\left((A_{10}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes 10\right)\sqcup\left((A_{11}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes 11\right). (102)

There are two possibilities. Either all four affine subspaces Aσ′A_{\sigma}^{\prime} of 𝔽22​k−2\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} are distinct or they are not.

Suppose first that the affine subspaces Aσ′A_{\sigma}^{\prime} are not all distinct, so that there are A1′A_{1}^{\prime} and A2′A_{2}^{\prime} such that

A1′:=A11′=Aρ′,A2′:=Aσ′=Aτ′.\displaystyle A_{1}^{\prime}:=A_{11}^{\prime}=A_{\rho}^{\prime},\quad A_{2}^{\prime}:=A_{\sigma}^{\prime}=A_{\tau}^{\prime}. (103)

In this case, we use the fact that Rk−1⊔Sk−1=𝔽22​k−2R_{k-1}\sqcup S_{k-1}=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} to write

|A∩Rk|\displaystyle|A\cap R_{k}| =|A1′|+2⋅|A2′∩Rk−1|\displaystyle=|A_{1}^{\prime}|+2\cdot|A_{2}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1}| (104)
|A∩Sk|\displaystyle|A\cap S_{k}| =|A1′|+2⋅|A2′∩Sk−1|\displaystyle=|A_{1}^{\prime}|+2\cdot|A_{2}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1}| (105)

which, using our inductive hypothesis and dimAσ′=d−dimF=d−2\dim A_{\sigma}^{\prime}=d-\dim F=d-2 for all σ∈𝔽22\sigma\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2}, implies

|A∩Rk|\displaystyle|A\cap R_{k}| ≤2d−2+2⋅(2d−3+2k−2)=2d−1+2k−1\displaystyle\leq 2^{d-2}+2\cdot(2^{d-3}+2^{k-2})=2^{d-1}+2^{k-1} (106)
|A∩Sk|\displaystyle|A\cap S_{k}| ≤2d−2+2⋅(2d−3+2k−3)=2d−1+2k−2.\displaystyle\leq 2^{d-2}+2\cdot(2^{d-3}+2^{k-3})=2^{d-1}+2^{k-2}. (107)

Suppose now that the four affine subspaces Aσ′A_{\sigma}^{\prime} of 𝔽22​k−2\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} are all distinct. By Lemma III.1, the subspaces arise as translations of the same linear subspace W′⊂𝔽22​k−2W^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} of dimension dimW′=d−dimF=d−2\dim W^{\prime}=d-\dim F=d-2.

By combining A00′A_{00}^{\prime} and A01′A_{01}^{\prime} into (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional affine space A00,01′A_{00,01}^{\prime}, we can rewrite (101) as

A∩Rk=\displaystyle A\cap R_{k}= ((A00,01′∩Rk−1)⊗00)⊔((A10′∩Rk−1)⊗10)⊔((A11′∩Sk−1)⊗11)\displaystyle\left((A_{00,01}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes 00\right)\sqcup\left((A_{10}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1})\otimes 10\right)\sqcup\left((A_{11}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1})\otimes 11\right) (108)

which leads to

|A∩Rk|=|A00,01′∩Rk−1|+|A10′∩Rk−1|+|A11′∩Sk−1|.\displaystyle|A\cap R_{k}|=|A_{00,01}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1}|+|A_{10}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1}|+|A_{11}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1}|. (109)

If d=kd=k, then |A∩Rk|≤2d−1+2k−1=2d|A\cap R_{k}|\leq 2^{d-1}+2^{k-1}=2^{d}. For affine spaces with d>kd>k, we prove the upper bound on |A∩Rk||A\cap R_{k}| using Corollary III.1 with e=d−2e=d-2

|A∩Rk|\displaystyle|A\cap R_{k}| ≤2d−2+2k−2+2d−2+2k−2=2d−1+2k−1\displaystyle\leq 2^{d-2}+2^{k-2}+2^{d-2}+2^{k-2}=2^{d-1}+2^{k-1} (110)

where the Corollary’s assumption follows from the inductive hypothesis and Lemma E.1. The upper bound on |A∩Sk||A\cap S_{k}| follows from Corollary E.2 with e=d−2e=d-2

|A∩Sk|\displaystyle|A\cap S_{k}| =|A00′∩Sk−1|+|A01′∩Sk−1|+|A10′∩Sk−1|+|A11′∩Rk−1|≤2d−1+2k−2\displaystyle=|A_{00}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{01}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{10}^{\prime}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{11}^{\prime}\cap R_{k-1}|\leq 2^{d-1}+2^{k-2} (111)

where the Corollary’s assumption follows from the inductive hypothesis and Lemma E.1. ∎

Theorem III.4.

For any positive integer kk and any affine subspace A⊂𝔽22​kA\subset\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k} of dimension d=dimAd=\dim A, we have

|A∩Sk|≤{2dd<k2d−1+2k−2k≤d<2​k−122​k−2d=2​k−122​k−1−2k−1d=2​k|A\cap S_{k}|\leq\begin{cases}2^{d}&d<k\\ 2^{d-1}+2^{k-2}&k\leq d<2k-1\\ 2^{2k-2}&d=2k-1\\ 2^{2k-1}-2^{k-1}&d=2k\end{cases} (112)

where

Sk:={(x1,…,x2​k)∈𝔽22​k:∑i=1kxi​xi+k=1mod2}.S_{k}:=\left\{(x_{1},...,x_{2k})\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}:\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{i}x_{i+k}=1\mod 2\right\}. (113)
Proof.

The four upper bounds in (112) follow from Lemma E.1, Lemma III.3, Lemma E.3, and Corollary E.1, respectively. ∎

III.3 Asymptotic Classical Hardness of Twisted Bent Target OPI

Definition III.5.

Let R,μ∈(0,1)R,\mu\in(0,1) be constants. For each positive integer kk, we define the Twisted Bent Target OPI (TBT-OPI) problem as follows. let SkS_{k} be the set of eq (113). For each of the m=22​k−1m=2^{2k}-1 evaluation points α∈𝔽22​k∗\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_{2^{2k}}^{*}, let A∼GL2​k​(𝔽2)A\sim\mathrm{GL}_{2k}(\mathbb{F}_{2}) be a random independent invertible matrix and set

Fα=ϕ−1​(A​ϕ​(x)),F_{\alpha}=\phi^{-1}(A\phi(x)), (114)

where ϕ\phi is the bijection of eq (20). The (R,μ)(R,\mu)-TBT-OPI problem is to find a polynomial f⁡(X)f(X) of degree at most ⌈R⋅m⌉\lceil R\cdot m\rceil such that f⁡(α)∈Fαf(\alpha)\in F_{\alpha} for at least ⌊μ⋅m⌋\lfloor\mu\cdot m\rfloor distinct α\alpha.

Lemma III.6.

The TBT-OPI sets FαF_{\alpha} are efficiently constructible per requirement (2) of IV.2.

Proof.

Note that if A=IA=I, then applying a phase to SkS_{k} can be achieved with a single layer of transversal CZ gates. We can then change the basis to account for AA by conjugating this with a circuit of O​(k2)=O~​(1)O(k^{2})=\widetilde{O}(1) CNOT gates. ∎

Theorem III.7.

There exists a choice of constant R≈1/10R\approx 1/10 so that, letting μ=μD​Q​I:=12+R2​(1−R2)\mu=\mu_{DQI}:=\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{R}{2}\left(1-\frac{R}{2}\right)}, the number of trials of XP required to solve (R,μ)(R,\mu)-TBT-OPI (definition III.5) is at least exp⁡(0.02​m)\exp(0.02m).

Proof.

The number of trials that XP needs to beat DQI is 1γ\frac{1}{\gamma} where γ\gamma is the objective function of (). This objective function is upper bounded through a direct application the Hoeffding inequality [41] by (115):

ℙ⁡(∑i=1mXi≥t)≤exp⁡(−2​(t−𝔼⁡[∑i=1mXi])2m)\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_{i}\geq t\right)\leq\exp\left(-2\frac{(t-\mathbb{E}[\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_{i}])^{2}}{m}\right) (115)

IV Asymptotically Optimal Quantum Speedup

To achieve the speedup of Theorem I.1, we have to use methods for the circuit implementation that are not necessarily optimal at the smaller problem sizes we envision for near-term applications. We describe these alternative implementations in Section IV.1. Then in Section IV.2 we observe Theorem I.1 as a corollary of this implementation (on the quantum side) along with the lower bounds on runtime of XP that was shown in Theorem III.7.

IV.1 Asymptotically Optimal Implementation

While Section II focused on optimizing constant factors for finite-size implementations, we now analyze the asymptotic complexity of DQI applied to the OPI problem. We demonstrate that under certain conditions, the DQI algorithm can be implemented using a quantum circuit with a number of gates that is nearly linear in the problem size mm. We use the notation O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(m) to hide factors polylogarithmic in mm.

We first establish the complexity of the key algebraic subroutines required. These complexities are well-established in classical computer algebra and apply over arbitrary finite fields 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}.

Lemma IV.1 (Fast Algebraic Subroutines).

Let mm be the problem size parameter. The following tasks can be computed reversibly using O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(m) field operations in 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}:

  1. 1.

    Multipoint Polynomial Evaluation (MPE): Evaluating a polynomial of degree <m<m at mm points.

  2. 2.

    Reed-Solomon (RS) Decoding: Decoding an RS code of length mm up to half its minimum distance.

Proof.


  1. 1.

    Fast algorithms for MPE utilize a divide-and-conquer strategy. The complexity is O⁡(M⁡(m)​log⁡m)O(M(m)\log m) field operations, where M⁡(m)M(m) is the cost to multiply two degree mm polynomials [42, Chapter 10]. Since M​(m)=O~​(m)M(m)=\widetilde{O}(m) using fast multiplication algorithms [43, 44, 45], the total cost is O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(m) field operations.

  2. 2.

    The key equation for RS decoding can be solved using the Fast Extended Euclidean Algorithm (Fast EEA), which runs in O​(M​(m)​log⁡m)=O~​(m)O(M(m)\log m)=\widetilde{O}(m) field operations [42, Chapter 11]. Subsequent steps (root finding and error evaluation) also take O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(m) field operations using fast MPE [46].

These algorithms are algebraic and can be implemented reversibly on a quantum computer. ∎

We now analyze the overall complexity of DQI. The result depends critically on the efficiency of the objective function implementation and the size of the field relative to mm.

Theorem IV.2.

Consider the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} with mm constraints and n=R​mn=Rm variables (where R∈(0,1)R\in(0,1) is constant). The DQI algorithm can be implemented by a quantum circuit using O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(m) elementary quantum gates, provided that:

  1. 1.

    The field size qq satisfies log⁡q=O⁡(polylog⁡(m))\log q=O(\mathrm{polylog}(m)) (i.e., the bit length b=O~​(1)b=\widetilde{O}(1)).

  2. 2.

    The subsets FiF_{i} are structured such that an oracle UiU_{i} for objective function fif_{i}, defined as Ui​|x⟩=fi​(x)​|x⟩U_{i}\ket{x}=f_{i}(x)\ket{x}, can be implemented by a quantum circuit using O~​(1)\widetilde{O}(1) gates.

Proof.

We analyze the complexity of the DQI algorithm stages (as described in Section II.1). The conditions ensure that basic arithmetic operations (addition, multiplication) in 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} require O~​(b)=O~​(1)\widetilde{O}(b)=\widetilde{O}(1) gates. The degree of the enhancing polynomial is l=O⁡(n)=O⁡(m)l=O(n)=O(m).

  • •

    Stage 1: Dicke State Preparation. Standard dense Dicke state preparation requires O⁡(l​m)=O⁡(m2)O(lm)=O(m^{2}) gates [47]. To achieve near linear time, we describe a new Dicke State Preparation method in Section B.2, which employs a reversible implementation of a Divide and Conquer unranking strategy, accelerated by Binary Splitting. As analyzed in the appendix, the total gate complexity for this step is O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(m).

  • •

    Stage 2: Syndrome Computation. We analyze the complexity of the sequential approach described in Section II.1, but using dense Dicke States instead of sparse Dicke States. This stage iterates mm times. Below, we show that the cost of each iteration is O~​(1)\widetilde{O}(1) resulting in a total cost of O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(m) :

    • –

      Constraint Encoding and Error Generation (Apply GiG_{i}): The gate GiG_{i} can be implemented using QFTs over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} and one call to the oracle UiU_{i} [4, Section 14.4]. The cost of the QFT is O~​(b)=O~​(1)\widetilde{O}(b)=\widetilde{O}(1). By assumption, the cost of UiU_{i} is O~​(1)\widetilde{O}(1). Thus, the cost of GiG_{i} is O~​(1)\widetilde{O}(1).

    • –

      Syndrome Update: We update the syndrome register with BiT⋅eiB^{T}_{i}\cdot e_{i}. This involves one field multiplication and addition, costing O~​(1)\widetilde{O}(1) gates.

  • •

    Stage 3: Reversible Decoding. We reversibly decode the Reed-Solomon code C⟂C^{\perp}. By Lemma IV.1, this requires O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(m) field operations, resulting in O~​(m⋅b)=O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(m\cdot b)=\widetilde{O}(m) gates.

  • •

    Stage 4: Final Transformation (IQFT). Applying the inverse QFT over 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}. This takes O~​(n⋅b)=O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(n\cdot b)=\widetilde{O}(m) gates.

Total Complexity: Since each stage requires O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(m) gates, the total gate complexity of the DQI algorithm under the stated conditions is O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(m). ∎

The conditions required for Theorem IV.2 are met, for instance, when qq is small (e.g., the binary extension fields analyzed in this paper, provided bb is polylogarithmic in mm) and when the OPI instance has some special structure that allows for efficient constraint encoding. For example, in the Polynomial Approximation problem, the subsets FiF_{i} are contiguous intervals [48], allowing UiU_{i} to be implemented efficiently via comparators in O~​(b)\widetilde{O}(b) gates.

It is important to contrast this with the general OPI case studied in Section 5 of [4], where m≈qm\approx q and the subsets FiF_{i} are arbitrary.

Corollary IV.1.

Consider the general OPI problem over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} where m=q−1m=q-1 and the subsets FiF_{i} are arbitrary (e.g., the balanced case where |Fi|≈q/2|F_{i}|\approx q/2). The DQI algorithm requires O~​(m2)\widetilde{O}(m^{2}) elementary quantum gates.

Proof.

In this case, b=O​(log⁡m)=O~​(1)b=O(\log m)=\widetilde{O}(1). However, implementing the oracle UiU_{i} or the gate GiG_{i} for an arbitrary function defined by a subset of size O⁡(q)O(q) generally requires O~​(q)=O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(q)=\widetilde{O}(m) gates (e.g., using QROM or generic state preparation [27]). The total cost of Stage 2 (Constraint Encoding) becomes m⋅O~​(m)=O~​(m2)m\cdot\widetilde{O}(m)=\widetilde{O}(m^{2}), dominating the overall complexity. ∎

IV.2 Asymptotic Optimality

Combining Theorem IV.2 and Theorem III.7 we have Theorem I.1: See I.1 Since any quantum circuit of nn gates can be simulated in time O⁡(2n)O(2^{n}), our speedup provides the largest separation possible between classical and quantum runtimes. This is somewhat extraordinary since OPI is essentially a contrived problem and seems (to us) no more “quantum" or “natural" than e.g. factoring or period-finding. We speculate informally on the outlook for this situation below.

  • •

    Faster Classical Algorithms for OPI: Although the best attacks we are currently aware of for OPI take exponential time in the number of evaluation points, it is certainly possible that better algorithms exist. It is interesting to note that none of the algorithms we know about leverage the low-degree algebraic structure and instead treat it as an arbitrary max-LINSAT problem.

  • •

    Better Shor circuits: Assuming the speedup for OPI stands, we wonder if further ideas along the line of thinking of [5, 49] could culminate in an asymptotically-optimal speedup based on Shor’s algorithm.

  • •

    Peeling off log factors: Although we omit the polylogarithmic factors here, there is room to optimize them and we wonder whether such effort would reveal a more practically-usable speedup or merely complicate matters without much gain at useful problem scales.

V Resource Estimates

V.1 Logical Costs

To provide a concrete assessment of the resources required to solve an instance of OPI using DQI, we performed a detailed logical cost analysis of the complete, end-to-end algorithm. We implemented the key subroutines—including the RS Decoders using the Synchronized and Dialog based EEA methods (as detailed in Section II.2.2 and Section II.2.3), and the Sparse Dicke State Preparation from Appendix B; as a Bloq in the Qualtran quantum compilation framework [19] and used it to analyze the precise qubit and gate costs.

The results of this analysis are summarized in Table 6 for several representative instances of the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem. The table presents the total Toffoli and Clifford gate counts, the number of logical qubits required for the reversible decoder, and the estimated classical intractability of each instance. For G​F​(2b)GF(2^{b}), since multiplication by a constant field element requires only Clifford gates, for small n/mn/m it turns out to be better to spend a higher gate cost to run Zalka’s EEA and have explicit access to the Bézout coefficients such that the Chien search subroutine that evaluates the Bézout coefficient polynomial σ⁡(x)\sigma(x) at mm different constants, uses only Clifford gates. Using Dialogs, the EEA part is significantly cheaper than Zalka’s EEA, but because we only have implicit access to the polynomial σ⁡(x)\sigma(x), each evaluation of σ⁡(x)\sigma(x) and σ′​(x)\sigma^{\prime}(x) now requires applying the Dialog and uses quantum-quantum multiplication [8] of field elements instead of quantum-classical multiplication. For both the approaches, the qubit counts scale as 2​n​b+𝒪⁡(log2⁡(n))2nb+\mathcal{O}(\log_{2}(n))

These resource estimates become particularly noteworthy when contextualized against other well-studied, classically intractable and verifiable optimization problems. Integer factorization using Shor’s algorithm serves as the canonical benchmark for large-scale quantum computation. As shown in the state-of-the-art estimates in [20], factoring a 2048-bit RSA integer is estimated to require approximately 6.5×1096.5\times 10^{9} Toffoli gates and 13991399 logical qubits, while factoring a 1024-bit RSA integer requiers 1.1×1091.1\times 10^{9} Toffoli gates and 742742 logical qubits. In comparison, several of our OPI instances that are well into the classically intractable regime (requiring >1023>10^{23} trials) and exhibit Toffoli counts that are about two to three orders of magnitude smaller, with logical qubit counts that are about two to three times higher.

V.2 Physical Costs

For estimating physical costs, we assume one large rectangular grid of physical qubits with nearest neighbor connections, a uniform gate error rate of 0.1%, a surface code cycle time of 1 microsecond, and a control system reaction time of 10 microseconds. With these assumptions, the imagined physical layout of the algorithm will consist of a compute region using hot storage and a memory region using cold storage. The compute region will store logical qubits “normally", as distance dd surface code patches using 2​(d+1)22(d+1)^{2} physical qubits. The cold storage memory region will store qubits more densely, by using 2D yoked surface codes [50]. Since our Toffoli gate counts are low enough, magic state cultivation [51] will suffice to prepare |T⟩\ket{T} states with low enough error rates, and thus we will not any dedicated space for magic state factories.

As an example, let us look at compiling the instance (m=4095,n=70,b=12)(m=4095,n=70,b=12). The dominant subroutines in the decomposition of the circuit are primitives to do arithmetic over Galois Field, like quantum-quantum multiplication (GF2Mul) and synthesizing a linear reversible circuit (SynthesizeLR) for quantum-classical multiplication and squaring. For these two primitives, we provide hand optimized lattice surgery layouts in Fig. 4 and Fig. 2 with magic state cultivation in-place.

Referring to [20, Figure 6], note that a distance 21 patch is sufficient for normal surface code patches to reach a per-patch per-round logical error rate of 10−1310^{-13}. So our hot patches will use 2⋅(21+1)2=9682\cdot(21+1)^{2}=968 physical qubits per logical qubit. For the cold storage, again referring to [20, Figure 6], yoking with a 2D parity check code reaches a logical error rate of 10−1310^{-13} when using 350350 physical qubits per logical qubit. So cold logical qubits will be roughly triple the density of hot logical qubits. For (m=4095,n=70,b=12)(m=4095,n=70,b=12), the algorithm uses 18851885 logical qubits. We propose to allocate a 40×4840\times 48 cold storage region with 19201920 logical qubits using 2D Yoked Surface codes. We also propose a thin 3×40=1203\times 40=120 qubit hot storage region. Our mockup for GF multiplication for b=12b=12 fits in a 3×(2.5​b+9)=3×393\times(2.5b+9)=3\times 39 region, including ancilla patches and space needed for cultivation. Thus, our layout uses 120×968+1920×350≈800​k120\times 968+1920\times 350\approx 800k physical qubits. A mockup of the high-level spacial layout is shown in Fig. 5.

Now let’s come to time. In the decomposition of logical circuit for (m=4095,n=70,b=12)(m=4095,n=70,b=12), there are 5821558215 calls to GF2Mul and 687564687564 calls to SynthesizeLR. We define the Parity Control Toffoli gate as a generalization of the Toffoli gate that computes the Boolean AND of the XOR of a subset of controls and updates a subset of targets [52, Figure 1]; we employ such gates since they can be implemented efficiently using lattice surgery Fig. 3. Our GF2Mul compilation from Fig. 4 requires 1.5​d1.5d rounds per Parity Control Toffoli gate (PCTOF). For b=12b=12, using optimized GF2 arithmetic circuits from Appendix C, there are 5151 PCTOF gates. Therefore, it takes 1.5⋅51≈77​d1.5\cdot 51\approx 77d rounds for one quantum-quantum multiplication of field elements. For SynthesizeLR, we present a hand-optimized layout in Fig. 2 that takes 10​d10d rounds and 3×233\times 23 surface code patches for b=12b=12. Therefore, with d=21d=21, these two combined give us 58215⋅77⋅21+687564⋅10⋅21=2.4×10858215\cdot 77\cdot 21+687564\cdot 10\cdot 21=2.4\times 10^{8}. To provide a conservative estimate of the total runtime, we multiply this number by a factor of four: doubling it once to account for overhead from other smaller operations and routing, and doubling it a second time to account for the time needed to move qubits between cold and hot storage. Thus, we estimate a total of 1×1091\times 10^{9} rounds. We need to protect 1920+120=20401920+120=2040 logical qubits for a total of 1×1091\times 10^{9} rounds. With an LER of 10−1310^{-13}, this gives us a no-logical-error shot rate of plattice surgery=(1−10−13)2040⋅1⋅109=(1−10−13)2×1012≈81.5%p_{\text{lattice surgery}}=(1-10^{-13})^{2040\cdot 1\cdot 10^{9}}=(1-10^{-13})^{2\times 10^{12}}\approx 81.5\% and a per shot runtime of  1616 minutes. To account for error due to cultivation, we cultivate |T⟩\ket{T} states with a fidelity of 2×10−92\times 10^{-9}. For a total Toffoli count of 5.72×1065.72\times 10^{6}, this gives us a pcultivation=(1−2×10−9)4×5.72×106≈95.5%p_{\text{cultivation}}=(1-2\times 10^{-9})^{4\times 5.72\times 10^{6}}\approx 95.5\%. Combining the two success probabilities above, we have a per-shot success rate of pcultivation×plattice surgery≈77.9%p_{\text{cultivation}}\times p_{\text{lattice surgery}}\approx 77.9\%, which means about 4 retries are sufficient for boosting the probability of a successful shot close to 1. Therefore, the total runtime would be ≈1\approx 1 hour.

To summarize, we estimate that solving a classically intractable instance of the OPI problem using DQI requires ≈800​k\approx 800k physical qubits and ≈1\approx 1 hour of runtime. This estimate assumes a quantum computer with a surface code cycle time of 1 microsecond, a control system reaction time of 10 microseconds, a square grid of qubits with nearest neighbor connectivity, and a uniform depolarizing noise model with a noise strength of 1 error per 1000 gates.

VI Conclusion

This work establishes Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) applied to the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem as a landmark candidate for practical quantum advantage. From a complexity-theoretic perspective, we have shown that DQI+OPI is the first known proposal for verifiable superpolynomial speedup that achieves optimal asymptotic efficiency, requiring only O~​(N)\widetilde{O}(N) quantum gates to solve instances with classical hardness O⁡(2N)O(2^{N}). This matches the theoretical lower bound and significantly outperforms the asymptotic scaling of Shor’s algorithm for cryptography.

The realization of this speedup relies on the concrete efficiency of the underlying reversible Reed-Solomon (RS) decoder. We introduced a suite of novel algorithmic and compilation techniques targeting the Extended Euclidean Algorithm (EEA), the critical bottleneck in RS decoding. Our innovations, including the Dialog representation for implicit Bézout coefficient access and optimized in-place register sharing architectures, rigorously reduce the space complexity to the theoretical minimum of 2​n​b2nb qubits while substantially lowering gate counts. These techniques are broadly applicable and promise significant improvements for other quantum algorithms reliant on the EEA, particularly those for Elliptic Curve Cryptography.

We provided a comprehensive end-to-end compilation and resource analysis for DQI, focusing on OPI over binary extension fields G​F​(2b)GF(2^{b}). We analyzed the classical hardness against tailored attacks, such as the Extended Prange algorithm, and identified resilient instances based on bent functions. Our concrete resource estimates demonstrate that DQI can solve instances requiring >1023>10^{23} classical trials using approximately 5.72 million Toffoli gates and 1885 logical qubits. This represents a reduction of three orders of magnitude in the gate count compared to breaking RSA-2048. Furthermore, our physical resource analysis, supported by hand-optimized lattice surgery layouts for key primitives, estimates that such instances could be solved on a fault-tolerant architecture with 800,000800,000 physical qubits in ≈1\approx 1 hour of runtime.

While our results position DQI as a compelling pathway for demonstrating quantum advantage in optimization, several avenues for future research remain.

Continued refinement of the classical hardness analysis is crucial. While we have demonstrated resilience against the best known classical attacks in the low-rate approximation regime, further investigation into the impact of sophisticated algebraic attacks ([40]) and establishing formal average-case hardness guarantees remain important open problems.

On the quantum side, there are a few routes to improved performance as well. In [54], a few interesting ideas were proposed. Among these was the idea to use Guruswami-Sudan and Koetter-Vardy list decoding algorithms for RS codes [55, 56]. This would allow us to find solutions that would take exponential time even with DQI and the Berlekamp-Massey decoder, with the cost of a higher (still polynomial) quantum circuit complexity. In a concurrent work, [15] considers applying DQI to algebraic geometry codes. These codes have some potentially favorable properties for verifiable quantum advantage demonstrations. Notably, they can maintain a constant rate and relative distance with considerably smaller (and in some cases constant) alphabet sizes than Reed-Solomon codes, which could improve the space footprint of the syndrome registers.

The Dialog representation introduced here opens new theoretical and practical questions regarding linear representations of numbers and polynomials. Key open questions include:

  1. 1.

    Can the size of the Dialog be reduced from ≈2​n\approx 2n field elements to ≈n\approx n when one of the inputs to the GCD is known classically?

  2. 2.

    Is there an efficient, in-place algorithm for transforming the Dialog for xx into the Dialog for x−1x^{-1}, or for computing the Dialog of x+yx+y from the Dialogs of xx and yy, without passing through the standard polynomial representation?

  3. 3.

    Are there more efficient linear representations beyond those based on the GCD algorithm, potentially enabling parallelization?

By bridging complexity theory with concrete algorithmic engineering, this work identifies and enables an asymptotically optimal and practically efficient route toward verifiable quantum advantage.

Appendix A Optimizing the number of trials of Extended Prange

Recall the optimization problem from Section III.2

maximize\displaystyle\mathrm{maximize}\,\,\, ℙ⁡(∑i=1mXi≥t)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_{i}\geq t\right)
subject​to\displaystyle\mathrm{subject\,to}\,\,\, Xi∼Ber⁡(P⁡[si])\displaystyle X_{i}\sim\mathrm{Ber}(P[s_{i}])
∑i=1msi≤B\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}s_{i}\leq B
0≤si≤b\displaystyle 0\leq s_{i}\leq b
ℙ⁡(1|s)≤ℙ⁡(1|s+1)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(1|s)\leq\mathbb{P}(1|s+1) (118)

Eq () is hard to solve exactly for large m,b,m,b, and BB, but using dynamic programming we can compute a tight approximation. To compute this approximation we note that eq () is invariant under permutations of sis_{i} which allows us to build the solution in any order we desire.

Before we describe our approach we note that any constructive that chooses the sis_{i} values iteratively faces the problem of given s1⋯sks_{1}\cdots s_{k} choose the best sk+1s_{k+1} which is a hard question since the sequence of sis_{i} induce a probability distribution and the set of probability distributions is intrinsically an unordered set. However, given our objective we can impose a few ordering relations with various degrees of effectiveness.

To solve the problem we employ a knapsack like dynamic programming approach. Dynamic programming is a constructive paradigm and since we are building an approximation algorithm the order we choose sis_{i} affects the quality of the result. Eq (120) shows that as we construct our solution the joint probability distribution induced by our choices of sis_{i} flows in the direction of increasing ∑Xi\sum X_{i}. We also note that the change in the joint distribution from ℙ(∙|s1⋯sk)\mathbb{P}(\bullet|s_{1}\cdots s_{k}) to ℙ(∙|s1⋯sksk+1)\mathbb{P}(\bullet|s_{1}\cdots s_{k}s_{k+1}) is controlled by ℙ⁡(1|sk+1)\mathbb{P}(1|s_{k+1}) which from eq (118) is monotonic, from these two observation we find that it is advantageous to choose the sis_{i} values in descending order s1≥s2≥⋯≥sms_{1}\geq s_{2}\geq\cdots\geq s_{m}. The advantage of this ordering is two folds, the first is that after the first few choices of sis_{i} the joint probability distribution stabilizes from one choice to another, the second is computational since it reduces the runtime of the algorithm.

ℙ(∑i=1k+1Xi≥t|s1⋯sksk+1)=ℙ(∑i=1kXi≥t|s1⋯sk)+ℙ(1|sk+1)ℙ(∑i=1kXi=t−1|s1⋯sk)\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}X_{i}\geq t|s_{1}\cdots s_{k}s_{k+1}\right)=\\ \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}X_{i}\geq t|s_{1}\cdots s_{k}\right)+\mathbb{P}\left(1|s_{k+1}\right)\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}X_{i}=t-1|s_{1}\cdots s_{k}\right)\\ (120)

Our solution has a dynamic programming state of (i,budget,low)(i,\mathrm{budget},\mathrm{low}) which means for the first ii variables and budget budget≤B\mathrm{budget}\leq B and ∀j≤isj≥low\forall_{j\leq i}s_{j}\geq\mathrm{low} what is the best joint probability distribution. This state has only two transitions (i,budget,low)→(i,budget,low+1)(i,\mathrm{budget},\mathrm{low})\to(i,\mathrm{budget},\mathrm{low}+1) and (i,budget,low)→(i−1,budget−low,low)(i,\mathrm{budget},\mathrm{low})\to(i-1,\mathrm{budget}-\mathrm{low},\mathrm{low}). To compare between the up to two probability distributions we get from these transitions we used two comparison functions.

The first comparison function is eq (122), which is quick and for most test cases we generated was at most 5%5\% lower than the optimal result with some outliers with a bigger error. The second is eq (123) which is slower since it involves computing the convolution between the probability distribution induced by our tuple s1⋯sks_{1}\cdots s_{k} and the one induced by the sequence computed by eq (124). The intuition behind FF which is computed using the classical dynamic programming knapsack algorithm is that we are doing a look ahead trying to estimate the best probability distribution given the remaining budget, but for computational reasons instead of solving the original problem we solve the related easier problem of maximizing the sum of probabilities, this gives us a better lower bound on the best final joint probability distribution starting from the given SS. Note that, eq (122) is a special case of eq (123) since it can be interpreted as the convolution of the current probability distribution with the probability distribution ℙ⁡(0)=1\mathbb{P}(0)=1.

T⁡(S)=(ℙ⁡(∑Xi≥t|S),ℙ⁡(∑Xi=t−1|S),ℙ⁡(∑Xi=t−2|S),⋯,ℙ⁡(∑Xi=0|S))T(S)=(\mathbb{P}(\sum X_{i}\geq t|S),\mathbb{P}(\sum X_{i}=t-1|S),\mathbb{P}(\sum X_{i}=t-2|S),\cdots,\mathbb{P}(\sum X_{i}=0|S)) (121)
S1≥S2⇔T⁡(S1)≥T⁡(S2)S_{1}\geq S_{2}\iff T(S_{1})\geq T(S_{2}) (122)
S1≥S2\displaystyle S_{1}\geq S_{2} ⇔T⁡(S1+F⁡(m−k,budget−∑s∈S1si,sk(1))≥T⁡(S2+F⁡(m−k,budget−∑s∈S2si),sk(2))CLOSE\displaystyle\iff T(S_{1}+F(m-k,\mathrm{budget}-\sum_{s\in S_{1}}s_{i},\ s_{k}^{(1)})\geq T(S_{2}+F(m-k,\mathrm{budget}-\sum_{s\in S_{2}}s_{i}),\ s_{k}^{(2)}) (123)

=(s1(1),⋯,sa(1),s1(2),⋯,sb(2))\displaystyle=(s_{1}^{(1)},\cdots,s_{a}^{(1)},s_{1}^{(2)},\cdots,s_{b}^{(2)})
F⁡(m,budget,low)\displaystyle F(m,\mathrm{budget},\mathrm{low}) =argmaxs1⋯sm∑i=1mP[si]\displaystyle=\mathrm{argmax}_{s_{1}\cdots s_{m}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}P[s_{i}]
subject​to\displaystyle\mathrm{subject\,to} ∑si≤budget\displaystyle\sum s_{i}\leq\mathrm{budget}
and\displaystyle\mathrm{and\ } si≥low\displaystyle s_{i}\geq\mathrm{low} (124)

We were unable to find a case where the dynamic programming approach with the slow sorting relation eq (123) disagrees with brute force solution. Although such cases theoretically exist we believe the error will be small. The time complexity of this solution is 𝒪⁡(m​b​B​t)\mathcal{O}(mbBt) with the fast sorting relation and 𝒪⁡(m​b​B​t2)\mathcal{O}(mbBt^{2}) with the slow sorting relation.

Appendix B Sparse Dicke State Preparation

The Dicke state |Dkm⟩\ket{D^{m}_{k}} is an equal weight superposition of all mm-qubit states with Hamming weight kk (i.e. all strings of length mm with exactly kk ones over a binary alphabet). As shown in Section II.1, to prepare the syndrome register for DQI, we need to prepare the state

∑k=0lwk​|Dkm⟩\sum_{k=0}^{l}w_{k}\ket{D^{m}_{k}}

where w0,w1,…,wl−1w_{0},w_{1},\dots,w_{l-1} where l=n/2l=n/2, are classically known coefficients and |Dkm⟩\ket{D^{m}_{k}} is the Dicke state

|Dkm⟩=1(mk)​∑|y|=k|y⟩\ket{D^{m}_{k}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{m}\choose{k}}}\sum_{|y|=k}\ket{y}

In the context of DQI, the Dicke state encodes a superposition over all possible (mk){m\choose k} error locations for 0≤k≤l0\leq k\leq l errors in a codeword of length mm. This encoding uses mm qubits. However, when m≫l=n/2m\gg l=n/2, we can define a sparse encoding that captures the same information using l×log2⁡ml\times\log_{2}{m} qubits, and thus be more space efficient.

A Sparse Dicke state |S​Dkm⟩\ket{SD^{m}_{k}} can be defined as a uniform superposition over all k−combinationsk-\text{combinations} of indices [1,2,…,m][1,2,\dots,m], stored using kk registers each of size b=⌈log2⁡(m+1)⌉b=\lceil\log_{2}{(m+1)}\rceil, using a total of k⋅bk\cdot b qubits.

|S​Dkm⟩=1(mk)∑1≤c1<c2<⋯<ck≤n|c1⟩b|c2⟩b⋯|ck⟩b\ket{SD^{m}_{k}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\binom{m}{k}}}\sum_{1\leq c_{1}<c_{2}<\dots<c_{k}\leq n}\ket{c_{1}}_{b}\ket{c_{2}}_{b}\cdots\ket{c_{k}}_{b}

First, we describe a way to prepare the Sparse Dicke states |S​Dkm⟩\ket{SD^{m}_{k}} using the Combinatorial Number System [57]. Then, we give two different constructions for quantum circuits to unrank combinations, one that minimizes the asymptotic complexity and other that minimizes the constant factors.

B.1 The unranking strategy

The Combinatorial Number System [57] defines an ordering over all (mk)\binom{m}{k} k−k-combinations such that a combination [ck,ck−1,…,c1][c_{k},c_{k-1},\dots,c_{1}] where n−1≥ck>ck−1>⋯>c1≥0n-1\geq c_{k}>c_{k-1}>\dots>c_{1}\geq 0 corresponds to a unique rank 0≤r<(mk)0\leq r<\binom{m}{k} given by the bijection

r=∑j=1k(cjj)r=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\binom{c_{j}}{j}

Using this bijection, the state preparation strategy involves two steps:

  1. 1.

    Prepare a uniform superposition of all ranks r∈{0,…,(mk)−1}r\in\{0,\dots,\binom{m}{k}-1\} using 𝒪⁡(k⋅b)\mathcal{O}(k\cdot b) gates [30]. Here we use the fact that (mk)≤mk\binom{m}{k}\leq m^{k}, so log2⁡(mk)≤k​log2​m=k⋅b\log_{2}{\binom{m}{k}}\leq k\log_{2}{m}=k\cdot b. The state of the system is given as follows.

    1(mk)​∑r=0(mk)−1|r⟩k⋅b\frac{1}{\sqrt{\binom{m}{k}}}\sum_{r=0}^{\binom{m}{k}-1}\ket{r}_{k\cdot b}
  2. 2.

    Apply a unitary transformation UUnrankU_{\text{Unrank}} that maps the rank rr to its corresponding combination C⁡(r)C(r):

    1(mk)​∑r|r⟩k⋅b→UUnrank1(mk)​∑r|C⁡(r)⟩k⋅b=|S​Dkm⟩\frac{1}{\sqrt{\binom{m}{k}}}\sum_{r}\ket{r}_{k\cdot b}\xrightarrow{U_{\text{Unrank}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\binom{m}{k}}}\sum_{r}\ket{C(r)}_{k\cdot b}=\ket{SD^{m}_{k}}

The efficiency of the state preparation is determined by the complexity of UUnrankU_{\text{Unrank}}.

B.2 Divide and Conquer Unranking for O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(m) Dicke State Preparation

We first describe a Divide and Conquer strategy for fast unranking. Given inputs (m,k,r)(m,k,r), we split the mm elements into two halves, M1M_{1} and M2M_{2}, of sizes m1=⌊m/2⌋m_{1}=\lfloor m/2\rfloor and m2=⌈m/2⌉m_{2}=\lceil m/2\rceil, and then calculate:

  1. 1.

    The number of elements k1k_{1} and k2k_{2} that the combination C⁡(r)C(r) selects from the first (M1M_{1}) and second halves (M2M_{2}) respectively, such that k1+k2=kk_{1}+k_{2}=k.

  2. 2.

    The residual ranks r1r_{1} and r2r_{2}, such that Cm,k​(r)=Cm1,k1​(r1)|Cm2,k2​(r2)C_{m,k}(r)=C_{m_{1},k_{1}}(r_{1})\|C_{m_{2},k_{2}}(r_{2}).

The unranking problem can then be solved by recursively solving the left and right subproblems for (m1,k1,r1)(m_{1},k_{1},r_{1}) and (m2,k2,r2)(m_{2},k_{2},r_{2}). If the work done at one level of recursion is W⁡(m,k)W(m,k), then the overall complexity of UUnrankU_{\text{Unrank}} follows the following recurrence relation:

T⁡(m,k)=T⁡(m/2,k1)+T⁡(m/2,k−k1)+W⁡(m,k)T(m,k)=T(m/2,k_{1})+T(m/2,k-k_{1})+W(m,k)

If we can show that W​(m,k)=O~​(m)W(m,k)=\widetilde{O}(m), then by Master Theorem (Case 2), the total complexity is T​(m,k)=O~​(m​log⁡m)T(m,k)=\widetilde{O}(m\log m), which is O~​(m)\widetilde{O}(m).

The number of ways to choose kk items such that exactly ii items come from M1M_{1} is given by the Hypergeometric distribution:

H⁡(i)=(m1i)​(m2k−i)H(i)=\binom{m_{1}}{i}\binom{m_{2}}{k-i}

To find the correct k1k_{1} for rank rr, we seek the value such that the prefix sum of H⁡(i)H(i) crosses rr:

P​S​(k1)=∑i=0k1−1H⁡(i)≤r<P​S​(k1+1)PS(k_{1})=\sum_{i=0}^{k_{1}-1}H(i)\leq r<PS(k_{1}+1)

We can find k1k_{1} using a binary search in O⁡(log⁡k)O(\log k) steps, provided we can efficiently calculate the prefix sum P​S​(x)PS(x). Once k1k_{1} is found, we calculate the residual ranks r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} corresponding to the left and right subproblems (via division and modulo operations on r−P​S​(k1)r-PS(k_{1})), and recursively solve them.

The efficiency of this approach hinges on the fast calculation of the Hypergeometric prefix sum P​S​(x)PS(x). The numbers involved (ranks and binomial coefficients) have bit length L=O⁡(k​log⁡m)L=O(k\log m). A naive summation of O⁡(k)O(k) terms is too slow. We use a technique called Binary Splitting. This method is effective for evaluating series where the ratio of consecutive terms R⁡(i)=H⁡(i+1)/H⁡(i)R(i)=H(i+1)/H(i) is a simple rational function of ii:

R⁡(i)=(m1−i)​(k−i)(i+1)​(m2−k+i+1)R(i)=\frac{(m_{1}-i)(k-i)}{(i+1)(m_{2}-k+i+1)}

The prefix sum can be written as P​S​(x)=H⁡(0)⋅(1+R⁡(0)+R⁡(0)​R​(1)+…)PS(x)=H(0)\cdot(1+R(0)+R(0)R(1)+\dots). Binary Splitting recursively computes this expression in a balanced tree structure. Crucially, it leverages fast integer multiplication algorithms (e.g., Schönhage–Strassen), which multiply LL-bit numbers in time O~​(L)\widetilde{O}(L). The total time complexity for calculating P​S​(x)PS(x) using Binary Splitting is thus O~​(L​log⁡k)=O~​(k​log⁡m)\widetilde{O}(L\log k)=\widetilde{O}(k\log m).

The divide and conquer algorithm can be implemented as a reversible quantum circuit UUnrankU_{\text{Unrank}}.

  1. 1.

    Reversible Fast Arithmetic: We require efficient reversible quantum circuits for fast integer multiplication and division that maintain the O~​(L)\widetilde{O}(L) complexity for arithmetic over LL bit integers.

  2. 2.

    Reversible Binary Splitting (UB​SU_{BS}): The Binary Splitting procedure is implemented reversibly using the fast arithmetic circuits. The gate complexity of UB​SU_{BS} is O~​(k​log⁡m)\widetilde{O}(k\log m).

  3. 3.

    Reversible Search: The binary search for k1k_{1} is implemented using the reversible Bit-wise Quantum Search strategy. This requires O⁡(log⁡k)O(\log k) coherent calls to UB​SU_{BS}.

The work done at one level of the recursion, W⁡(m,k)W(m,k), is dominated by the reversible search:

W⁡(m,k)=O⁡(log⁡k)⋅Cost​(UB​S)=O~​(k​log⁡m)=O~​(m)W(m,k)=O(\log k)\cdot\text{Cost}(U_{BS})=\widetilde{O}(k\log m)=\widetilde{O}(m)

B.3 Iterative Unranking for low constant factor Dicke State Preparation

The divide and conquer strategy described has optimal asymptotic complexity but would not be ideal for a constant factor analysis. Here, we describe a simple greedy algorithm to find the k−k-combination corresponding to rank rr with small constant factors: take ckc_{k} maximal with (ckk)≤r\binom{c_{k}}{k}\leq r, then take ck−1c_{k-1} maximal with (ck−1k−1)≤r−(ckk)\binom{c_{k-1}}{k-1}\leq r-\binom{c_{k}}{k}, and so on. We can translate this greedy algorithm into a reversible quantum circuit to prepare Sparse Dicke states using 2⋅k⋅b+b2\cdot k\cdot b+b qubits and 𝒪(m.k+k2b2)\mathcal{O}(m.k+k^{2}b^{2}) Toffoli gates as follows:

  1. 1.

    The unitary UUnrank​(n,k)U_{\text{Unrank}}(n,k) can be defined as a product of kk unitaries, each of which iteratively finds the jjth coefficient cjc_{j} in the sequence C⁡(r)C(r) as follows:

    UUnrank​(m,k)=Usearch​(m,1)⋅Usearch​(m,2)​…​Usearch​(m,k−1)⋅Usearch​(m,k)U_{\text{Unrank}}(m,k)=U_{\text{search}}(m,1)\cdot U_{\text{search}}(m,2)\dots U_{\text{search}}(m,k-1)\cdot U_{\text{search}}(m,k)

    Here Usearch​(m,j)U_{\text{search}}(m,j) can be defined as:

    Usearch​(m,j)​|r⟩j​log2​m​|0⟩log2⁡m→|r−(cjj)⟩(j−1)​log2​m​|cj⟩log2⁡mU_{\text{search}}(m,j)\ket{r}_{j\log_{2}{m}}\ket{0}_{\log_{2}{m}}\rightarrow\ket{r-\binom{c_{j}}{j}}_{(j-1)\log_{2}{m}}\ket{c_{j}}_{\log_{2}{m}}
  2. 2.

    The unitary Usearch​(m,j)U_{\text{search}}(m,j) can be implemented using a bitwise binary search strategy, where we determine the largest cjc_{j} such that (cjj)≤r\binom{c_{j}}{j}\leq r, iterating over log2⁡m\log_{2}{m} bits of cjc_{j} from most significant bit to least significant bit, and for each log2⁡m≥i≥0\log_{2}{m}\geq i\geq 0, set cj=cj+2ic_{j}=c_{j}+2^{i} if (cj+2ij)≤r\binom{c_{j}+2^{i}}{j}\leq r. A reversible quantum circuit would therefore require log2⁡(m)\log_{2}(m) calls to a sparse QROM, the iith of which loads 2i2^{i} binomial coefficients of the form (cj+2ij)\binom{c_{j}+2^{i}}{j}. The total Toffoli cost of the sparse QROMs across all iterations is therefore k.mk.m. Once the Binomial coefficients are loaded using the QROM, we also need a k.log2⁡mk.\log_{2}{m} comparator for each of the log2⁡m\log_{2}{m} bits of cjc_{j}. The total Toffoli cost of the comparators across all iterations is therefore 𝒪⁡((k​log2​m)2)\mathcal{O}((k\log_{2}{m})^{2}).

Appendix C Improved arithmetic circuits for binary extension fields

C.1 Parity Control Toffoli P​C​T​O​FPCTOF and Parity CNOT P​C​N​O​TPCNOT

The parity control Toffoli PCTOF is equivalent to a multi-target Toffoli gate with controls being the parity of a subset of qubits. The PCNOT gate is a CNOT gate that computes the XOR of its controls and is equivalent to a series of CNOTs with the same target. The main advantages of the PCNOT gate is that in the presence of enough ancillae, it can be performed in a single cycle using lattice surgery independent of the number of controls.

When the two control sets of a PCTOF are disjoint, as is the case of GF(2m)(2^{m}) multiplication, the two control parities can be computed in a single cycle. Fig. 6 shows the first PCTOF of Fig. 7 expanded in terms of PCNOT and Toffoli and in terms of CNOT and Toffoli gates.

C.2 GF(2m2^{m}) arithmetic circuits

Our implementation of the DQI algorithm relies on arithmetic circuits over GF field sizes of 2102^{10} through 2122^{12}. The bottleneck is GF multiplication.

To implement the respective multiplication (and division) circuits, we rely on [9]. This synthesis algorithm develops a modification of Karatsuba multiplication over a carefully selected irreducible polynomial, along with local optimizations using templates, allowing for a reduction in both Toffoli and CNOT gate counts compared to the state-of-the-art straight Karatsuba multiplication [8]. We tune the implementation [9] to focus on optimizing an ∞\infty-to-1 weighted sum of Toffoli and CNOT gate counts to utilize the PCTOF gates better. To get constructions made of the PCTOF and CNOT gates, we start from the Toffoli and CNOT circuits from [9] and commute the CNOT gates to the left while updating the sets of the PCTOF gates, resulting in circuits that start with three disjoint CNOT stages acting on the two input registers and the resulting register followed by a circuit made of the PCTOF gates. The first two CNOT circuits are equivalent to the identity since we do not modify the input registers and the CNOT circuit acting on the target can be ignored since the target is always initialized in the zero state. The resulting optimized circuits are summarized in Table 7. Fig. 7 shows the G​F​(23)GF(2^{3}) multiplication circuit with irreducible polynomial x3+x+1x^{3}+x+1 in terms of PCTOF gates and explicit circuit files are available as a part of the Zenodo upload of this paper.

In addition, we developed a circuit optimization method applicable to the kinds of circuits with PCTOF gates considered. The optimization algorithm relies on two observations: first, any two PCTOF gates commute, and second, each PCTOF gate computes a Boolean polynomial of degree 2 and then EXORs it onto a separate output register. This means that a single PCTOF gate can be thought of as a vector in the m2m^{2}-dimensional Boolean space, where each coordinate corresponds to a Boolean product of some two variables, and circuits with kk PCTOF gates (with targets on the bottom register such as in our case of GF multiplication circuits) can be thought of as k×m2k\,{\times}\,m^{2} matrices. This means that the matrix rank determines the minimal number of PCTOF gates necessary, in a given set that implements the desired functionality. We implemented this optimization algorithm and found a small optimization compared to what is directly offered by [9] (compare Toffoli count to the PCTOF count in Table 7). We suspect that the improvement is small due to the large number of optimizations that already went into [9].

C.3 Measurement-based Uncomputation for GF2 Multiplication.

The GF(2m)(2^{m}) multiplication operation is an out-of-place operation that applies the transformation |x⟩​|y⟩​|0⟩→|x⟩​|y⟩​|x​y⟩\ket{x}\ket{y}\ket{0}\rightarrow\ket{x}\ket{y}\ket{xy}. The uncomputation of this operation can be done using only measurements and C​ZCZ gates.

The uncomputation starts by measuring the target register in the XX basis. This is equivalent to applying the H⊗mH^{\otimes m} to the target register and then measuring in the computational basis. The H⊗mH^{\otimes m} operations transform the state to |x⟩​|y⟩​|x​y⟩=∑ai,j​|i⟩​|j⟩​|i​j⟩→H⊗m12m​∑c=02m−1{∑(−1)h⁡(c,i​j)​|i⟩​|j⟩}​|c⟩\ket{x}\ket{y}\ket{xy}=\sum a_{i,j}\ket{i}\ket{j}\ket{ij}\xrightarrow{H^{\otimes m}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{m}}}\sum_{c=0}^{2^{m}-1}\big\{\sum(-1)^{h(c,ij)}\ket{i}\ket{j}\big\}\ket{c} where h⁡(a,b)h(a,b) is the Hamming weight of a⊕ba\oplus b. After the measurement, we end up with a classical bitstring cc and phase flips on some of the coefficients of the input superposition ∑(−1)h⁡(c,i​j)​ai,j​|i⟩​|j⟩\sum(-1)^{h(c,ij)}a_{i,j}\ket{i}\ket{j}.

While it seems that we need to know the product to correct the phase, the linearity of hh and symmetry of C​ZCZ allow us to correct the phase with only C​ZCZs. For example if ct=1c_{t}{=}1 then we need to apply C​Z​(xi,yj)CZ(x_{i},y_{j}) for all (i,j)(i,j) pairs such that xi+jmodp⁡(x)x^{i+j}\mod p(x) has xtx^{t} where p⁡(x)p(x) is the irreducible polynomial. This leads to the requirement to implement a certain C​ZCZ gate circuit. Note that any such circuit can be implemented in depth ⌊m/2+0.4993⋅log2⁡(m)+3.0191⋅log⁡(m)−10.9139⌋\lfloor m/2+0.4993{\cdot}\log^{2}(m)+3.0191{\cdot}\log(m)-10.9139\rfloor, using no more than m2/4+O⁡(m​log2⁡(m))m^{2}/4+O(m\log^{2}(m)) Clifford gates [58] or O⁡(m2/log⁡(m))O(m^{2}/\log(m)) gates asymptotically.

Our implementation of measurement-based uncomputation of GF2 multiplication is available in Qualtran [19] as GF2MulMBUC and Fig. 8 shows the uncomputation of GF2 multiplication for m=3m{=}3 and irreducible polynomial x3+x+1x^{3}+x+1.

Appendix D Bounding the number of iterations for Synchronized Reversible Polynomial EEA

We analyze the worst-case number of iterations required for the synchronized, reversible implementation of the Polynomial Extended Euclidean Algorithm (PEEA) presented in Section II.2.2. This implementation utilizes shared registers and a 4-stage synchronized architecture designed to allow computation branches in a superposition to proceed efficiently at their own pace.

Let the input polynomials be AA and BB over a finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, with n=deg⁡(A)n=\deg(A) and deg⁡(B)<n\deg(B)<n.

Definition D.1 (Iteration Dynamics).

For iteration ii (which computes quotient QiQ_{i}, remainder RiR_{i}, and cofactor UiU_{i}):

  • •

    di=deg⁡(Qi)d_{i}=\deg(Q_{i}). We define d0=0d_{0}=0. Since deg⁡(B)<deg⁡(A)\deg(B)<\deg(A), di≥1d_{i}\geq 1 for i≥1i\geq 1.

  • •

    si=deg⁡(Ri−1)−deg⁡(Ri)s_{i}=\deg(R_{i-1})-\deg(R_{i}): The degree reduction of the remainder. si≥1s_{i}\geq 1.

Let kk be the total number of iterations. Let Dk=∑i=1kdiD_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i} and Sk=∑i=1ksiS_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}s_{i}.

Lemma D.2 (PEEA Constraints).

The variables are constrained by k≤Dkk\leq D_{k} and k≤Skk\leq S_{k}. For Full PEEA (coprime inputs, unequal degrees), Dk=nD_{k}=n and Sk=nS_{k}=n.

We analyze the time complexity TiT_{i} of iteration ii based on the 5 steps described in Fig. 9.

Lemma D.3 (Cost Per Iteration).

The number of cycles TiT_{i} required for iteration ii in the optimized implementation is Ti=2​di+si+di−1+2T_{i}=2d_{i}+s_{i}+d_{i-1}+2.

Proof.

We analyze the time required for each stage in the 4-stage cycle, corresponding to Steps 1-4 in Figure 1:

  1. 1.

    Stage 1 (Step-1, Poly Long Division): Time taken is the length of QiQ_{i} (number of terms), which is di+1d_{i}+1.

  2. 2.

    Stage 2 (Step-2, Remainder Normalization): Time taken is the total degree reduction sis_{i}.

  3. 3.

    Stage 3 (Step-3, Bézout Cofactor Alignment): Time taken is the degree growth from the prior iteration, di−1d_{i-1}.

  4. 4.

    Stage 4 (Step-4, Bézout Cofactor Update): Time taken is the length of QiQ_{i}, which is di+1d_{i}+1. The register swap (Step-5) occurs concurrently during the final cycle of this stage, incurring no extra time.

Summing the costs for iteration ii:

Ti\displaystyle T_{i} =(di+1)+si+di−1+(di+1)\displaystyle=(d_{i}+1)+s_{i}+d_{i-1}+(d_{i}+1)
=2​di+si+di−1+2.\displaystyle=2d_{i}+s_{i}+d_{i-1}+2.

∎

Lemma D.4 (Total Cost Function).

The total number of cycles TT required to complete kk iterations is T=3​Dk+Sk−dk+2​kT=3D_{k}+S_{k}-d_{k}+2k.

Proof.

The total time is the sum of TiT_{i} from i=1i=1 to kk.

T\displaystyle T =∑i=1kTi=∑i=1k(2​di+si+di−1+2)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}T_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(2d_{i}+s_{i}+d_{i-1}+2)
=2​∑i=1kdi+∑i=1ksi+∑i=1kdi−1+2​k.\displaystyle=2\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{k}s_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i-1}+2k.

We evaluate the third term: ∑i=1kdi−1=d0+d1+⋯+dk−1\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i-1}=d_{0}+d_{1}+\dots+d_{k-1}. Since d0=0d_{0}=0, this equals Dk−dkD_{k}-d_{k}.

T=2​Dk+Sk+(Dk−dk)+2​k=3​Dk+Sk−dk+2​k.T=2D_{k}+S_{k}+(D_{k}-d_{k})+2k=3D_{k}+S_{k}-d_{k}+2k.

We analyze the maximum cycles required for the Full PEEA, assuming worst-case coprime inputs with degrees (n,n−1)(n,n-1).

The maximum number of cycles required for the optimized synchronized Full PEEA on inputs of unequal degrees (max degree nn) is Tm​a​x=6​n−1T_{max}=6n-1.

+ω⁡(a,x)+ω⁡(b,x)+ω⁡(c,x)+𝟙Sk​(x)\displaystyle+\omega(a,x)+\omega(b,x)+\omega(c,x)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(x) (165)

which means that

𝟙Sk​(a+x)+𝟙Sk​(a+b+x)+𝟙Sk​(a+c+x)+𝟙Sk​(a+b+c+x)=ω⁡(b,c).\displaystyle\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+x)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+b+x)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+c+x)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+b+c+x)=\omega(b,c). (166)

Thus, for any fixed a,b,c∈𝔽22​ka,b,c\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k}, we can infer 𝟙Sk​(a+b+c+x)\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+b+c+x) from 𝟙Sk​(a+x)\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+x), 𝟙Sk​(a+b+x)\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+b+x), and 𝟙Sk​(a+c+x)\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+c+x). Indeed, if ω⁡(b,c)=0\omega(b,c)=0, then for every x∈Wx\in W we have the following eight equivalences

(a+x∈Rk)∧(a+b+x∈Rk)∧(a+c+x∈Rk)⇔a+b+c+x∈Rk\displaystyle(a+x\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+x\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+x\in R_{k})\iff a+b+c+x\in R_{k} (167)
(a+x∈Rk)∧(a+b+x∈Rk)∧(a+c+x∈Sk)⇔a+b+c+x∈Sk\displaystyle(a+x\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+x\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+x\in S_{k})\iff a+b+c+x\in S_{k} (168)
(a+x∈Rk)∧(a+b+x∈Sk)∧(a+c+x∈Rk)⇔a+b+c+x∈Sk\displaystyle(a+x\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+x\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+x\in R_{k})\iff a+b+c+x\in S_{k} (169)
(a+x∈Rk)∧(a+b+x∈Sk)∧(a+c+x∈Sk)⇔a+b+c+x∈Rk\displaystyle(a+x\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+x\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+x\in S_{k})\iff a+b+c+x\in R_{k} (170)
…\displaystyle\quad\quad\ldots
(a+x∈Sk)∧(a+b+x∈Sk)∧(a+c+x∈Sk)⇔a+b+c+x∈Sk.\displaystyle(a+x\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+x\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+x\in S_{k})\iff a+b+c+x\in S_{k}. (171)

If on the other hand ω⁡(b,c)=1\omega(b,c)=1, then for every x∈Wx\in W we have the eight equivalences

(a+x∈Rk)∧(a+b+x∈Rk)∧(a+c+x∈Sk)⇔a+b+c+x∈Rk\displaystyle(a+x\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+x\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+x\in S_{k})\iff a+b+c+x\in R_{k} (173)
(a+x∈Rk)∧(a+b+x∈Sk)∧(a+c+x∈Rk)⇔a+b+c+x∈Rk\displaystyle(a+x\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+x\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+x\in R_{k})\iff a+b+c+x\in R_{k} (174)
(a+x∈Rk)∧(a+b+x∈Sk)∧(a+c+x∈Sk)⇔a+b+c+x∈Sk\displaystyle(a+x\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+x\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+x\in S_{k})\iff a+b+c+x\in S_{k} (175)
…\displaystyle\quad\quad\ldots
(a+x∈Sk)∧(a+b+x∈Sk)∧(a+c+x∈Sk)⇔a+b+c+x∈Rk.\displaystyle(a+x\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+x\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+x\in S_{k})\iff a+b+c+x\in R_{k}. (176)

In either case, WW can be partitioned into eight disjoint sets

Wr​r​r\displaystyle W_{rrr} :={w∈W|(a+w∈Rk)∧(a+b+w∈Rk)∧(a+c+w∈Rk)}\displaystyle:=\{w\in W\,|\,(a+w\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+w\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+w\in R_{k})\} (177)
Wr​r​s\displaystyle W_{rrs} :={w∈W|(a+w∈Rk)∧(a+b+w∈Rk)∧(a+c+w∈Sk)}\displaystyle:=\{w\in W\,|\,(a+w\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+w\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+w\in S_{k})\} (178)
Wr​s​r\displaystyle W_{rsr} :={w∈W|(a+w∈Rk)∧(a+b+w∈Sk)∧(a+c+w∈Rk)}\displaystyle:=\{w\in W\,|\,(a+w\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+w\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+w\in R_{k})\} (179)
Wr​s​s\displaystyle W_{rss} :={w∈W|(a+w∈Rk)∧(a+b+w∈Sk)∧(a+c+w∈Sk)}\displaystyle:=\{w\in W\,|\,(a+w\in R_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+w\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+w\in S_{k})\} (180)
…\displaystyle\ldots
Ws​s​s\displaystyle W_{sss} :={w∈W|(a+w∈Sk)∧(a+b+w∈Sk)∧(a+c+w∈Sk)}\displaystyle:=\{w\in W\,|\,(a+w\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a+b+w\in S_{k})\,\land\,(a+c+w\in S_{k})\} (181)

so that W=Wr​r​r⊔Wr​r​s⊔…⊔Ws​s​sW=W_{rrr}\sqcup W_{rrs}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup W_{sss}. Consider the following disjoint unions of these sets

Wx​x​y\displaystyle W_{xxy} :=Wr​r​r⊔Wr​r​s⊔Ws​s​r⊔Ws​s​s\displaystyle:=W_{rrr}\sqcup W_{rrs}\sqcup W_{ssr}\sqcup W_{sss} (182)
Wx​x¯​y\displaystyle W_{x\overline{x}y} :=Wr​s​r⊔Wr​s​s⊔Ws​r​r⊔Ws​r​s\displaystyle:=W_{rsr}\sqcup W_{rss}\sqcup W_{srr}\sqcup W_{srs} (183)
Wx​y​y\displaystyle W_{xyy} :=Wr​r​r⊔Wr​s​s⊔Ws​r​r⊔Ws​s​s\displaystyle:=W_{rrr}\sqcup W_{rss}\sqcup W_{srr}\sqcup W_{sss} (184)
Wx​y​y¯\displaystyle W_{xy\overline{y}} :=Wr​r​s⊔Wr​s​r⊔Ws​r​s⊔Ws​s​r.\displaystyle:=W_{rrs}\sqcup W_{rsr}\sqcup W_{srs}\sqcup W_{ssr}. (185)

The indicator function of Wx​x¯​yW_{x\overline{x}y} restricted to WW is

𝟙Wx​x¯​y​(x)\displaystyle\mathbb{1}_{W_{x\overline{x}y}}(x) =𝟙Rk​(a+x)⋅𝟙Sk​(a+b+x)⋅𝟙Rk​(a+c+x)+𝟙Rk​(a+x)⋅𝟙Sk​(a+b+x)⋅𝟙Sk​(a+c+x)\displaystyle=\mathbb{1}_{R_{k}}(a+x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+b+x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{R_{k}}(a+c+x)+\mathbb{1}_{R_{k}}(a+x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+b+x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+c+x) (186)
+𝟙Sk(a+x)⋅𝟙Rk(a+b+x)⋅𝟙Rk(a+c+x)+𝟙Sk(a+x)⋅𝟙Rk(a+b+x)⋅𝟙Sk(a+c+x)\displaystyle+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{R_{k}}(a+b+x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{R_{k}}(a+c+x)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{R_{k}}(a+b+x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+c+x) (187)
=𝟙Rk​(a+x)⋅𝟙Sk​(a+b+x)+𝟙Sk​(a+x)⋅𝟙Rk​(a+b+x)\displaystyle=\mathbb{1}_{R_{k}}(a+x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+b+x)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{R_{k}}(a+b+x) (188)
=(1+𝟙Sk​(a+x))⋅𝟙Sk​(a+b+x)+𝟙Sk​(a+x)⋅(1+𝟙Sk​(a+b+x))\displaystyle=\left(1+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+x)\right)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+b+x)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+x)\cdot\left(1+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+b+x)\right) (189)
=𝟙Sk​(a+x)+𝟙Sk​(a+b+x)\displaystyle=\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+x)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(a+b+x) (190)
=𝟙Sk​(b)+ω⁡(a,b)+ω⁡(b,x)\displaystyle=\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(b)+\omega(a,b)+\omega(b,x) (191)

which is an affine functional on WW. Therefore, Wx​x¯​yW_{x\overline{x}y} is empty or an affine subspace of WW. So is Wx​x​yW_{xxy} whose indicator function restricted to WW is 𝟙Wx​x​y​(x)=𝟙Wx​x¯​y​(x)+1\mathbb{1}_{W_{xxy}}(x)=\mathbb{1}_{W_{x\overline{x}y}}(x)+1. Similarly, the indicator function of Wx​y​y¯W_{xy\overline{y}} restricted to WW is 𝟙Wx​y​y¯​(x)=𝟙Sk​(b)+𝟙Sk​(c)+ω⁡(a,b+c)+ω⁡(b+c,x)\mathbb{1}_{W_{xy\overline{y}}}(x)=\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(b)+\mathbb{1}_{S_{k}}(c)+\omega(a,b+c)+\omega(b+c,x) which is also an affine functional on WW. Moreover, (184) and (185) imply that Wx​y​y⊔Wx​y​y¯=WW_{xyy}\sqcup W_{xy\overline{y}}=W.

We can write

|A00∩Sk|=|Ws​r​r|+|Ws​r​s|+|Ws​s​r|+|Ws​s​s|\displaystyle|A_{00}\cap S_{k}|=|W_{srr}|+|W_{srs}|+|W_{ssr}|+|W_{sss}| (192)
|A01∩Sk|=|Wr​s​r|+|Wr​s​s|+|Ws​s​r|+|Ws​s​s|\displaystyle|A_{01}\cap S_{k}|=|W_{rsr}|+|W_{rss}|+|W_{ssr}|+|W_{sss}| (193)
|A10∩Sk|=|Wr​r​s|+|Wr​s​s|+|Ws​r​s|+|Ws​s​s|\displaystyle|A_{10}\cap S_{k}|=|W_{rrs}|+|W_{rss}|+|W_{srs}|+|W_{sss}| (194)

irrespective of ω⁡(b,c)\omega(b,c), so that

|A00∩Sk|+|A01∩Sk|+|A10∩Sk|\displaystyle|A_{00}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{01}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{10}\cap S_{k}| (195)
=|Wr​r​s|+|Wr​s​r|+2⋅|Wr​s​s|+|Ws​r​r|+2⋅|Ws​r​s|+2⋅|Ws​s​r|+3⋅|Ws​s​s|\displaystyle=|W_{rrs}|+|W_{rsr}|+2\cdot|W_{rss}|+|W_{srr}|+2\cdot|W_{srs}|+2\cdot|W_{ssr}|+3\cdot|W_{sss}|

also irrespective of ω⁡(b,c)\omega(b,c). The analogous expression for |A11∩Rk||A_{11}\cap R_{k}| depends on the value of ω⁡(b,c)\omega(b,c). We consider both cases constructing a pair of suitable affine spaces B1B_{1} and B2B_{2} for each one in turn.

First, if ω⁡(b,c)=0\omega(b,c)=0, then

|A11∩Rk|=|Wr​r​r|+|Wr​s​s|+|Ws​r​s|+|Ws​s​r|\displaystyle|A_{11}\cap R_{k}|=|W_{rrr}|+|W_{rss}|+|W_{srs}|+|W_{ssr}| (196)

and adding (195) yields

|A00∩Sk|+|A01∩Sk|+|A10∩Sk|+|A11∩Rk|\displaystyle|A_{00}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{01}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{10}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{11}\cap R_{k}| (197)
=|Wr​r​r|+|Wr​r​s|+|Wr​s​r|+3⋅|Wr​s​s|+|Ws​r​r|+3⋅|Ws​r​s|+3⋅|Ws​s​r|+3⋅|Ws​s​s|\displaystyle=|W_{rrr}|+|W_{rrs}|+|W_{rsr}|+3\cdot|W_{rss}|+|W_{srr}|+3\cdot|W_{srs}|+3\cdot|W_{ssr}|+3\cdot|W_{sss}| (198)
=|W|+2⋅(|Wr​s​s|+|Ws​r​s|+|Ws​s​r|+|Ws​s​s|).\displaystyle=|W|+2\cdot\left(|W_{rss}|+|W_{srs}|+|W_{ssr}|+|W_{sss}|\right). (199)

Define

B1\displaystyle B_{1} :=(a+b+Wx​x¯​y)⊔(a+c+Wx​x​y)\displaystyle:=(a+b+W_{x\overline{x}y})\sqcup(a+c+W_{xxy}) (200)
B2\displaystyle B_{2} :=(a+b+Wx​x​y)⊔(a+c+Wx​x¯​y)\displaystyle:=(a+b+W_{xxy})\sqcup(a+c+W_{x\overline{x}y}) (201)

so that B1⊔B2B_{1}\sqcup B_{2} is an affine space of dimension dimW+1\dim W+1 and

|B1|\displaystyle|B_{1}| =|W|\displaystyle=|W| (202)
|B2∩Sk|\displaystyle|B_{2}\cap S_{k}| =|Wr​s​s|+|Ws​r​s|+|Ws​s​r|+|Ws​s​s|\displaystyle=|W_{rss}|+|W_{srs}|+|W_{ssr}|+|W_{sss}| (203)

and hence

|A00∩Sk|+|A01∩Sk|+|A10∩Sk|+|A11∩Rk|=|B1|+2⋅|B2∩Sk|.\displaystyle|A_{00}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{01}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{10}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{11}\cap R_{k}|=|B_{1}|+2\cdot|B_{2}\cap S_{k}|. (204)

Now, if ω⁡(b,c)=1\omega(b,c)=1, then

|A11∩Rk|=|Wr​r​s|+|Wr​s​r|+|Ws​r​r|+|Ws​s​s|\displaystyle|A_{11}\cap R_{k}|=|W_{rrs}|+|W_{rsr}|+|W_{srr}|+|W_{sss}| (205)

and adding (195) yields

|A00∩Sk|+|A01∩Sk|+|A10∩Sk|+|A11∩Rk|\displaystyle|A_{00}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{01}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{10}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{11}\cap R_{k}| (206)
=2⋅|Wr​r​s|+2⋅|Wr​s​r|+2⋅|Wr​s​s|+2⋅|Ws​r​r|+2⋅|Ws​r​s|+2⋅|Ws​s​r|+4⋅|Ws​s​s|.\displaystyle=2\cdot|W_{rrs}|+2\cdot|W_{rsr}|+2\cdot|W_{rss}|+2\cdot|W_{srr}|+2\cdot|W_{srs}|+2\cdot|W_{ssr}|+4\cdot|W_{sss}|.

Redefine

B1\displaystyle B_{1} :=(a+Wx​y​y¯)⊔(a+b+Wx​y​y¯)\displaystyle:=(a+W_{xy\overline{y}})\sqcup(a+b+W_{xy\overline{y}}) (207)
B2\displaystyle B_{2} :=(a+Wx​y​y)⊔(a+b+Wx​y​y)\displaystyle:=(a+W_{xyy})\sqcup(a+b+W_{xyy}) (208)

so that B1⊔B2B_{1}\sqcup B_{2} is again an affine space of dimension dimW+1\dim W+1 and

|B1|\displaystyle|B_{1}| =2⋅|Wr​r​s|+2⋅|Wr​s​r|+2⋅|Ws​r​s|+2⋅|Ws​s​r|\displaystyle=2\cdot|W_{rrs}|+2\cdot|W_{rsr}|+2\cdot|W_{srs}|+2\cdot|W_{ssr}| (209)
|B2∩Sk|\displaystyle|B_{2}\cap S_{k}| =|Wr​s​s|+|Ws​r​r|+2⋅|Ws​s​s|\displaystyle=|W_{rss}|+|W_{srr}|+2\cdot|W_{sss}| (210)

and hence

|A00∩Sk|+|A01∩Sk|+|A10∩Sk|+|A11∩Rk|=|B1|+2⋅|B2∩Sk|\displaystyle|A_{00}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{01}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{10}\cap S_{k}|+|A_{11}\cap R_{k}|=|B_{1}|+2\cdot|B_{2}\cap S_{k}| (211)

completing the proof of the Lemma. ∎

We note the following conditional upper bound which is implied by Lemma E.4 and which will facilitate its use in an inductive proof.

Corollary E.2 (Bound for mixed recursive structure formulas with four terms).

Let ee and k>1k>1 be positive integers. If |B∩Sk−1|≤2dimB−1+2k−3|B\cap S_{k-1}|\leq 2^{\dim B-1}+2^{k-3} for every affine subspace BB of 𝔽22​k−2\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} with dimB∈{e,e+1}\dim B\in\{e,e+1\}, then

|A00∩Sk−1|+|A01∩Sk−1|+|A10∩Sk−1|+|A11∩Rk−1|≤2e+1+2k−2\displaystyle|A_{00}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{01}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{10}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{11}\cap R_{k-1}|\leq 2^{e+1}+2^{k-2} (212)

for any four disjoint affine subspaces of the form

A00\displaystyle A_{00} =a+W\displaystyle=a+W (213)
A01\displaystyle A_{01} =a+b+W\displaystyle=a+b+W (214)
A10\displaystyle A_{10} =a+c+W\displaystyle=a+c+W (215)
A11\displaystyle A_{11} =a+b+c+W\displaystyle=a+b+c+W (216)

arising as translations of the same ee-dimensional linear subspace W⊂𝔽22​k−2W\subset\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} with a,b,c∈𝔽22​k−2a,b,c\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2}.

Proof.

By Lemma E.4, there exist two sets B1B_{1} and B2B_{2} each of which is either empty or affine and such that

|A00∩Sk−1|+|A01∩Sk−1|+|A10∩Sk−1|+|A11∩Rk−1|=|B1|+2⋅|B2∩Sk−1|\displaystyle|A_{00}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{01}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{10}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{11}\cap R_{k-1}|=|B_{1}|+2\cdot|B_{2}\cap S_{k-1}| (217)

and such that |B1|+|B2|=2⋅|W||B_{1}|+|B_{2}|=2\cdot|W|. Thus, if B1=∅B_{1}=\emptyset, then B2B_{2} is an affine subspace of 𝔽22​k−2\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} of dimension e+1e+1 and using the assumption in the Corollary, we obtain

|A00∩Sk−1|+|A01∩Sk−1|+|A10∩Sk−1|+|A11∩Rk−1|≤0+2⋅(2e+2k−3)=2e+1+2k−2.\displaystyle|A_{00}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{01}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{10}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{11}\cap R_{k-1}|\leq 0+2\cdot(2^{e}+2^{k-3})=2^{e+1}+2^{k-2}. (218)

If B2=∅B_{2}=\emptyset, then B1B_{1} is an affine subspace of 𝔽22​k−2\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2k-2} of dimension e+1e+1. Therefore,

|A00∩Sk−1|+|A01∩Sk−1|+|A10∩Sk−1|+|A11∩Rk−1|≤2e+1+2⋅0<2e+1+2k−2.\displaystyle|A_{00}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{01}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{10}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{11}\cap R_{k-1}|\leq 2^{e+1}+2\cdot 0<2^{e+1}+2^{k-2}. (219)

Finally, if neither B1B_{1} nor B2B_{2} is empty, then both are affine and dimB1=dimB2=e\dim B_{1}=\dim B_{2}=e. Therefore,

|A00∩Sk−1|+|A01∩Sk−1|+|A10∩Sk−1|+|A11∩Rk−1|≤2e+2⋅(2e−1+2k−3)=2e+1+2k−2\displaystyle|A_{00}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{01}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{10}\cap S_{k-1}|+|A_{11}\cap R_{k-1}|\leq 2^{e}+2\cdot(2^{e-1}+2^{k-3})=2^{e+1}+2^{k-2} (220)

completing the proof of the Corollary. ∎

Appendix F Reference Python Implementation

F.1 Reed Solomon Decoding using Synchronized EEA for Explicit Bézout coefficients

Fig. 9 gives our optimized implementation of Zalka’s synchronized reversible EEA [12]. Fig. 10 uses this as a subroutine and shows how to implement the Chien Search [23] and Forney’s algorithm [24] steps for syndrome decoding of Reed Solomon codes, given the shared in-place register representation of the error locator polynomial σ⁡(z)\sigma(z) and error evaluator polynomial Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z).

F.2 Reed Solomon Decoding using Dialog based EEA for Implicit Bézout Coefficients

Fig. 11 gives our optimized implementation of constructing a Dialog based on the Bernstein-Yang GCD algorithm [17] using a shared register representation to save space. We also show how once can consume the Dialog to perform modular multiplication or modular division. Fig. 12 uses uses the Dialog based EEA for syndrome decoding of Reed Solomon codes, and shows how one can evaluate the error locator polynomial σ⁡(z)\sigma(z) and it’s derivative σ′​(z)\sigma^{\prime}(z), given access to the Dialog of σ⁡(z)\sigma(z).
